title: The Standards
text:
Your grade in this course is built from the standards below. Each is a specific, demonstrable skill, marked met or not yet — there is no partial credit. Standards can be demonstrated (and re-demonstrated) through homework cycles, the in-class checkpoints (weeks 4, 6, 8, 10 — see grading), activity work, the design project, and the final defense. Convergent standards require at least one in-class demonstration. A standard missed in week 4 and nailed in week 11 is met.
Each standard carries a tag:

title: The Standards
section: Fetch — get real data in and out
text:
Fetch — get real data in and out
F1 — Acquire real data from a phone sensor, a file, or a keyless API. divergent
F2 — Read data’s shape: recognize CSV rows/columns and JSON/dictionary structure, and pull out the value you want. convergent

title: The Standards
section: Process — turn raw data into meaning
text:
Process — turn raw data into meaning
P1 — Write and reuse a function, and check it in isolation against a hand estimate. convergent (At least one P1 demonstration is hand-written at a checkpoint: a short function from a given spec, no AI — the minimum writing fluency that verification rests on.)
P2 — Run a parameter sweep: one function across many values, results written to a file. convergent
P3 — Tame a large dataset with pandas: filter, summarize, reduce many rows to a few meaningful numbers. convergent
P4 — Read code well enough to predict what a short script does, and recognize the shape of a computational project (inputs → script → outputs). convergent
P5 (proposed — under discussion) — Hold a whole project in your head: navigate a multi-file program you produced, and explain what each piece does, why it is structured that way, and what breaks if an input is malformed. divergent


P5 is what the final defense tests. P4 is reading a paragraph; P5 is knowing your way around the whole book.

title: The Standards
text:
Simulate — build models, make predictions
S1 — Build a model of a simple system: a given algebraic relation, or by time-stepping. convergent
S2 — Decide what to include and what to ignore: identify a model’s assumptions and judge whether they’re reasonable for the situation. divergent
S3 — Judge whether to trust the model: recognize the ways it goes wrong — too coarse a step (numerical), a missing effect (physical), or use outside its valid range (extrapolation). convergent
S4 — Explore with a model: pose a what-if, vary inputs, and interpret how the output responds. divergent

title: The Standards
section: Analyze — and the habits woven through everything
text:
Analyze — and the habits woven through everything
A1 — Estimate and sanity-check a result before trusting it. convergent
A2 — Make and judge an honest plot, and catch a misleading one. convergent
A3 — State uncertainty and document provenance: report how far model and reality diverge without false precision, and record where a number came from so someone else could rerun it. divergent
A4 — Direct and audit AI: get an AI to produce a computational artifact and critically audit the output. divergent

title: Peer evaluation
text: The design project is team-built, but this course certifies individuals — so the engagement credits earned during the project period (pin-ups #1 and #2 at 3 each, the mock defense at 2 — 8 credits total) are awarded per person, informed by your teammates’ evaluations. This page is the whole system; there are no hidden rubrics.

title: Peer evaluation
text:
How it works
You complete two short evaluations of your teammates — five minutes each, on Canvas:

Evaluation 1, end of week 13 — formative. Nothing is scaled by it; its results reach me only, and its purpose is early warning. A team drifting toward a passenger problem finds out in week 13, when the fix is a conversation, not in finals week, when the fix is a grade.
Evaluation 2, finals week — summative. This one informs the project-period credits.

Both ask the same three questions, and notice they ask for descriptions, not scores:

For each teammate: describe, concretely, what they built, verified, or produced. (“Wrote and annotated the filtering module; ran the dt-halving checks” — that kind of concrete.)
For each teammate: describe one moment they moved the team forward.
Anything I should know? (Free response, optional.)

title: Peer evaluation
text:
What happens with it
The default outcome — by far the most common — is nothing. Ordinary evaluations, including honest ones mentioning ordinary friction, change no one’s credits. This is not a ranking exercise, there is no quota of criticism, and teams where everyone worked are teams where everyone keeps their 8 credits.
The instrument exists for one pattern: a teammate no one can describe. When multiple evaluations independently can’t answer question 1 about the same person — nothing built, nothing verified, nothing to point at — that person and I have a conversation, and their project-period credits can be reduced, in the worst case to zero. A single evaluator’s account is never acted on alone; convergence across teammates is the standard, and the conversation always precedes the consequence.

title: Peer evaluation
text:
Why descriptions instead of ratings
Because ratings inflate — nobody wants to give a teammate a 3/5, so everyone gets 5s and the instrument reads nothing. Descriptions resist inflation for a simple reason: you can’t describe work that didn’t happen. A hollow answer to “what did they build?” isn’t an accusation anyone had to make; it’s just an absence, visible on its own. This also protects you as an evaluator — you’re never asked to judge a teammate, only to state what you saw, which is a much easier thing to do honestly.

title: Peer evaluation
text:
The honest framing
This is not surveillance and it’s not a gotcha — it’s the standard mechanism (borrowed from decades of team-based-learning practice) that makes team projects fair to the people who do the work. If you’re worried about it, notice what it actually takes to be unaffected: do something your teammates can name. That is the lowest bar in the course, and it’s identical to the bar your first job will set. And if you’re on the other side — carrying a teammate and quietly resenting it — evaluation 1 is your pressure valve, weeks before it costs anyone anything.






Note



Team conflict that’s bigger than this instrument — someone unreachable, someone hostile, a team genuinely stuck — should not wait for an evaluation window. Come talk to me at any desk crit, or email. The evaluations are the formal channel; they were never meant to be the only one.

title: Project studio
text: No new reading for two weeks. Class becomes studio: your team building a real computational project at the tables, instructors circulating, and structured critique events where the work goes public. This page is the operating manual.

title: Project studio
text:
The project
Your team (3–4, formed at launch) picks from the menu:

Audio forensics — load a recording, process the signal, extract something real: the frequency of a passing siren (and hence, Doppler willing, its speed), the tempo of a song, the echo delay of a room.
Video tracking — track an object through video frames (trackpy) and turn pixels into physics: a projectile’s drag, a pendulum’s damping, a teammate’s gait.
Live-data instrument — build on week 8: fetch from an API or phone sensor on a schedule, process the stream, produce an auto-updating analysis (ISS pass predictor, weather-trend monitor, stairwell-step counter).
Design-space explorer — a serious parameter sweep of a real system (heat sink, bike frame member, pump selection) culminating in a “here is the best design and why” recommendation.
Industry option — a problem provided by an external partner, scope negotiated at launch. (Menu subject to expansion; pitch me your own at launch if you have one — the bar is “genuinely multi-file, genuinely verifiable.”)

Deliverables, due finals week: (1) the code — a real multi-file program, every file annotated; (2) the spec history — your prompts and specifications as they evolved, kept as you go, not reconstructed; (3) verification evidence — hand checks, test cases, sanity arguments, honestly including the ones that failed; (4) a short published report — a Quarto page presenting the problem, method, results, and uncertainty (A2 and A3 on full display).

title: Project studio
text:
Desk crits (Tuesdays)
Instructors and TAs circulate table to table, ~10 focused minutes per team. The rule that makes desk crits work: bring your ugliest problem, not your best work. A desk crit spent showing off is a wasted desk crit; the ten minutes exist to unstick the thing that’s stuck. Have ready: what you’re trying to do, what’s happening instead, and what you’ve already tried (that last one is the difference between a consultation and a rescue).

title: Project studio
text:
Pin-ups (Thursdays)
Work goes up — screens turned outward or printouts on the wall — and tables review each other’s projects in rotation.
Pin-up #1 (week 12): specs and verification plans. Before major code exists, the thinking gets critiqued: is the specification complete? What did they assume (S2)? How will they know it works (the verification plan)? Catching a spec hole in week 12 costs a conversation; catching it in week 14 costs your weekend.
Pin-up #2 (week 13): working artifacts. Running code, real output, draft plots. Now the critique vocabulary is the standards page itself — the divergent standards are the review questions: What’s assumed (S2)? How was it verified (A1/A4)? Is the plot honest (A2)? Could I rerun this from what’s documented (A3)?
Critique etiquette, which is itself being practiced (engineers review each other’s work for a living, and doing it well is a career skill): critique the work, never the people; questions beat verdicts (“what happens if the input file is empty?” beats “this seems fragile”); every critique names one thing that’s working, specifically; and “cleanest” claims must be defended with criteria — matches the spec, verified, honest about uncertainty, rerunnable — not vibes.

title: Project studio
text:
The divergence rule
Teams that chose the same menu item will have produced different programs — different architectures, different assumptions, sometimes different answers from similar data. Pin-up #2 deliberately pairs same-project teams: first each explains the other team’s architecture back to them (a brutal and wonderful P4 exercise), then the argument: which choices were better, and by what criterion? This is the “everyone used AI and the results came out different — now understand why” engine, running at full scale, on work you care about.

title: Project studio
text:
Individual accountability — read this twice
Divide the labor. Do not divide the understanding. The defense (week 14 and finals) is individual, and it will ask you about parts of the project you didn’t personally produce — that’s not a gotcha, it’s the definition of being on an engineering team. The cheapest insurance is built into the deliverables: the annotation discipline (every file annotated in the team’s own words) plus a standing team habit worth stealing — end each studio session with five minutes of “walk me through what you did today.” A teammate who can’t explain a file to you in week 12 is a teammate who can’t explain it to me in finals, and you now share that problem. One more structural fact: project-period engagement credits are individual, informed by peer evaluation — description-based and default-harmless; read that page rather than the rumor of it.

title: Project studio
text:
Standards in play
Everything, but the center of gravity: S2, S4, A2, A3, A4 through the deliverables and pin-ups, and above all P5 — holding a whole project in your head — which these two weeks exist to build and the defense exists to measure.

title: Simulate II: assumptions, trust & what-ifs
text: Last week you built the machine. This week: judgment — what to put in it, when to believe it, and how to ask it questions. This is the most engineering week of the course; there is exactly one line of new code in it.

title: Simulate II: assumptions, trust & what-ifs
text:
Think First
Recall

Week 9’s coffee model: name two real physical effects it completely ignored. Did the answer seem to suffer?
Week 1: “have intuition about the physics” was called an old skill with renewed importance. This is the week that cashes that check.

Look Ahead

“All models are wrong; some are useful.” How can both halves be true at once?
A model matched every test you ran. A colleague wants to use it 20% outside the range you tested. What do you say?

title: Simulate II: assumptions, trust & what-ifs
section: All models are wrong — on purpose
text:
All models are wrong — on purpose
The coffee model ignored evaporation, the mug’s heat capacity, the room warming slightly, stirring. Deliberately. A model is not a copy of reality; it’s a selective simplification, and the selection is the engineering. Include everything and you have an intractable mess; include too little and you have tidy nonsense. The skill (standard S2) is threefold: know what you included, know what you excluded, and know under what circumstances an exclusion stops being ignorable. Ignoring air drag on a dropped wrench: fine. On a dropped feather: absurd. On a wrench dropped from an airplane: the exclusion quietly became the answer.

title: Simulate II: assumptions, trust & what-ifs
text:
The assumptions audit
A concrete ritual for any model — yours or an AI’s. Three columns on paper: Included / Excluded / Excluded matters when… For projectile motion, the classic audit: constant gravity (excluded: variation with altitude — matters for rockets, not baseballs); no air drag (matters when speed is high, mass is low, or distances are long — i.e., for most real projectiles, which is why artillery tables existed); no spin (tell that to a golf ball); flat Earth (matters beyond a few km). Auditing takes five minutes, and it converts “the model said 47 meters” into “the model said 47 meters, and here’s the box that number lives inside” — which is the difference between a student answer and an engineering answer.

title: Simulate II: assumptions, trust & what-ifs
section: The three ways models fail — the full S3
text:
The three ways models fail — the full S3
Numerical — the discretization lies. Week 9’s too-big step: error you injected by chopping time into chunks. Diagnosis: halve the step, compare. You own this one already.
Physical — a missing effect bites. The model faithfully solves equations that no longer describe the situation: drag-free artillery, the coffee model applied to a mug sitting in sunlight. Diagnosis: the assumptions audit, plus comparison against even one real measurement.
Extrapolation — a good model, used outside its tested range. The most dangerous, because the model earned genuine trust inside its box and nothing visible changes when you step outside. The night before the Challenger launch, engineers had O-ring seal data from prior flights — the coldest around 12 °C. Launch morning was around 0 °C. The judgment call treated behavior beyond the data as if the trend politely continued. It did not. Seven people died, and “we had no data at that temperature” is now the textbook sentence every engineer is taught to say out loud, before the decision.






Important



The three failures have three different diagnostics — step-halving, assumptions audit, know-your-data-range — which is why S3 makes you name which kind of wrongness you suspect. “The model might be off” is a mood; “we’re extrapolating 12 degrees past our coldest data point” is an engineering statement.

title: Simulate II: assumptions, trust & what-ifs
section: What-if: the model as a question-answering machine
text:
What-if: the model as a question-answering machine
Now the payoff for all this discipline — the reason we build models at all. A trusted model is an experiment factory: what if the mug is thicker? The room colder? The tank valve half-open? Each what-if is a parameter sweep (week 5!) pointed at a simulation (week 9!):
for k in np.linspace(0.01, 0.10, 10):      # ten hypothetical mug/lid designs
    temps = simulate_cooling(k=k, dt=1.0)   # your week-9 machine, functionized
    plt.plot(time, temps, label=f"k={k:.2f}")
Ten futures, one plot, one second. The S4 skill isn’t running this — it’s interpreting it: which knob moves the output a lot (sensitive — measure it carefully, control it tightly) and which barely matters (insensitive — stop agonizing over it). Sensitivity is where simulations stop being homework and start being design.

title: Simulate II: assumptions, trust & what-ifs
text:
Interrogating an AI-built model
The AI will happily build any model you ask for — on assumptions it chooses and does not volunteer. Ask for “a projectile simulation” and drag is silently in or silently out, coin-flip. So the A4 workflow for models adds one prompt, always: “State every assumption this model makes and its valid range.” The reply is genuinely useful — and then you audit it too, because the model’s actual assumptions live in the code, not in the model’s self-description. (The code is the territory; the AI’s summary is a map drawn by an enthusiastic intern.) Assumptions audit, on everything, no exceptions — including, in week 14, on your own project, where the examiner will be me.

For a damped oscillator model — a mass on a spring with friction, position marched forward exactly like the coffee — commit on paper: (1) two assumptions you’d bet it makes; (2) for each, one situation where that assumption breaks; (3) a prediction with one sentence of physics: if the damping coefficient doubles, what happens to the motion? Thursday: model critique. Each table receives another table’s week-9 model plus its assumption audit, and reviews it S2/S3-style — is the audit honest? which failure mode is nearest? — before we vote on the damping question and settle it by running the sweep live.

title: Fetch: APIs, JSON, and your phone
text: Week 1’s third promise: reach out and touch the world. Today your programs stop living on hand-typed numbers and start consuming live reality — a spacecraft’s position, your own pocket’s accelerometer.

title: Fetch: APIs, JSON, and your phone
text:
Think First
Recall

Week 6: files are how programs talk to each other. What if the “other program” is on a computer on another continent?
Week 7’s F2 habit: what do you check about any data before computing with it?

Look Ahead

When an app shows you live weather, where is that number actually coming from?
If you report “the ISS was over Boulder at 2:14 pm,” what would someone need to verify that claim?
crumbs: Fetch: APIs, JSON, and your phone

title: Fetch: APIs, JSON, and your phone
text:
What an API is
An API (application programming interface) is, for our purposes, a program running on someone else’s computer that answers questions over the internet. Your code sends a request to a URL; their computer sends back a response full of data. That’s the entire mental model — the web, minus the pretty pages, machine to machine.
import requests
r = requests.get("https://api.wheretheiss.at/v1/satellites/25544")
info = r.json()
print(info)
Three lines, and info now holds the live position of the International Space Station. (25544 is the ISS’s catalog number; this API needs no account or key, which is why it’s our classroom workhorse.)
crumbs: Fetch: APIs, JSON, and your phone

title: Fetch: APIs, JSON, and your phone
section: JSON: the shape of the response
text:
JSON: the shape of the response
What comes back looks like this:
{"name": "iss", "latitude": 40.11, "longitude": -105.32,
 "altitude": 421.4, "velocity": 27571.8, "timestamp": 1760040000}
That’s JSON — curly braces, "key": value pairs — and Python receives it as a dictionary: like an array, but indexed by name instead of position. Pulling out the value you want (the F2 skill, new costume):
lat = info["latitude"]
speed = info["velocity"]     # km/h — 27,572 km/h. Check that against intuition: orbit in ~90 min.
Real APIs nest structures — a dictionary containing lists containing dictionaries — and the skill is navigating the shape: print the whole thing once, find your target visually, then write the path to it, e.g. data["hourly"]["temperature"][0]. Never guess a key name; look, then extract.


Sanity check, A1-style: Earth’s circumference is ~40,000 km. At 27,600 km/h, one lap is ~87 minutes. The ISS orbits in about 90. The API is telling the truth.
crumbs: Fetch: APIs, JSON, and your phone

title: Fetch: APIs, JSON, and your phone
section: Loop it: from a number to a dataset
text:
Loop it: from a number to a dataset
One request is a snapshot. A loop is an instrument:
import time
rows = []
for k in range(20):
    info = requests.get("https://api.wheretheiss.at/v1/satellites/25544").json()
    rows.append([info["timestamp"], info["latitude"], info["longitude"]])
    time.sleep(30)                 # be polite: one request every 30 s
Ten minutes of this and you have the ISS ground track — which is a pandas DataFrame and a week-6 plot away from being your orbital dataset. Every tool in this course is now composing: fetch (this week) → process (weeks 3–7) → analyze (week 6). Simulate joins next week.






Important



That time.sleep(30) is not decoration. A loop without it hammers a free public server many times per second — rude at best, a denial-of-service at worst, and the fastest way to get the whole university’s network blocked. Fetching politely is part of the F1 standard, not an optional courtesy.
crumbs: Fetch: APIs, JSON, and your phone

title: Fetch: APIs, JSON, and your phone
section: Your phone is a lab instrument
text:
Your phone is a lab instrument
Your phone contains an accelerometer, gyroscope, magnetometer, barometer, GPS — a few hundred dollars of sensors you already own. Free apps (we’ll use Phyphox, built by physicists at RWTH Aachen) record them and export CSV — which, as of week 7, is a format you eat for breakfast. Thursday you’ll record your own walk down a stairwell and find the steps in the acceleration trace. This is F1 in its purest form: reality → file → your program, no intermediary.
crumbs: Fetch: APIs, JSON, and your phone

title: Fetch: APIs, JSON, and your phone
section: Provenance: where did this number come from?
text:
Provenance: where did this number come from?
New data sources make the A3 habit urgent. A number without provenance is a rumor; the difference is a recorded trail: which source (URL or instrument), when (timestamp — the ISS position is meaningless without it), what settings (sampling rate, phone orientation, which pocket). The professional standard is that someone else could re-fetch and re-run your analysis from your notes alone. Cheapest implementation: your fetching script writes the provenance into the output file — a header row or companion file with URL, query time, and parameters. The script that fetched the data documents the data. Let the computer keep the receipts.

On paper, sketch the JSON you’d expect from a weather API asked for current conditions in Boulder: invent the structure — keys, nesting, units — for at least temperature, wind, and time. There’s no wrong answer; there is a committed one. Thursday opens by querying a real weather API and comparing the class’s guesses to reality — the gaps (What timezone is that timestamp? Wind in m/s or mph? Says who?) are the whole lesson. Then: the stairwell lab. Wear pocketed pants.
crumbs: Fetch: APIs, JSON, and your phone

title: Data in, data out — and honest plots
text: Your sweep wrote a file last week. Today: why files are how programs remember and how they talk to each other — and then plotting, which is where computation meets ethics faster than you’d think.
crumbs: Data in, data out — and honest plots

title: Data in, data out — and honest plots
text:
Think First
Recall

When your Colab notebook closes, what happens to every variable in it?
Week 5’s sweep wrote sweep_results.csv. Who — or what — is that file for?

Look Ahead

Can a plot be technically accurate and still be a lie?
Why would an engineer look at raw data before computing anything with it?
crumbs: Data in, data out — and honest plots

title: Data in, data out — and honest plots
text:
Files: memory and interface
Programs are goldfish — every variable dies when the program ends. Files persist. But the deeper reason files matter in engineering: they’re how programs talk to each other. Your sweep’s CSV is a plotting script’s input. A test rig’s log file is your pandas script’s input (week 7). Your project’s output file is your teammate’s input (weeks 12–13). Inputs → script → outputs isn’t just the shape of one program — chained together, it’s the shape of an entire computational workflow, and recognizing that shape is standard P4.
crumbs: Data in, data out — and honest plots

title: Data in, data out — and honest plots
section: CSV: rows, columns, and a header
text:
CSV: rows, columns, and a header
Open last week’s output in a text editor and it’s just this:
height_m,fall_time_s
0.5,0.319
1.0,0.452
1.5,0.553
First row: header — column names. Every other row: one record, values separated by commas (hence the name). That’s the entire format. Reading it into Python:
import numpy as np
data = np.loadtxt("sweep_results.csv", delimiter=",", skiprows=1)
h = data[:, 0]     # all rows, column 0: the heights
t = data[:, 1]     # all rows, column 1: the fall times


data[:, 0] reads as “every row, first column.” Column counting starts at 0 — remember this in week 11, when MATLAB starts at 1 and the off-by-one trap opens for business.
The F2 skill is exactly this: look at a data file, recognize its shape, and pull out the value you want. Always look first — open the raw file, check the header, check the units (are they even stated? if not, that’s a provenance problem, see A3), check a couple of rows by eye — before computing anything.
crumbs: Data in, data out — and honest plots

title: Data in, data out — and honest plots
text:
Plotting
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
plt.plot(h, t, "o-")
plt.xlabel("Drop height (m)")
plt.ylabel("Fall time (s)")
plt.title("Fall time vs. height")
plt.grid(alpha=0.3)
plt.show()
Course law: an axis without a label and units is an unfinished plot, and unfinished plots don’t get submitted. Beyond that, one habit: after plotting, interrogate the shape. This one curves — flattening as height grows. Does that match physics? (\(t \propto \sqrt{h}\) — yes.) A plot is a verification instrument pointed at 100 rows at once; a sign error or unit slip that hides in a CSV is often visually obvious as a wrong shape.
crumbs: Data in, data out — and honest plots

title: Data in, data out — and honest plots
text:
The honest-plot doctrine
Now the part with ethical weight. These two plots show the same six data points — a motor’s efficiency measured monthly. And in the spirit of A3, this page practices what it preaches: the plots below are generated by the code you can unfold, at the moment this page was built — the figure and its provenance are the same artifact.

Show the code that made both plots
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

months = ["Jan","Feb","Mar","Apr","May","Jun"]
eff = np.array([94.1, 94.3, 94.2, 94.6, 94.5, 94.8])

# Version A — honest
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.2,3.4))
ax.plot(months, eff, "o-", color="#2b6cb0")
ax.set_ylim(0,100)
ax.set_ylabel("Motor efficiency (%)"); ax.set_xlabel("Month")
ax.set_title("Motor efficiency, Jan–Jun")
ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
plt.show()

# Version B — the same data, dressed to deceive
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.2,3.4))
ax.plot(months, eff, "o-", color="#c53030", linewidth=3)
ax.set_ylim(94.0, 94.9)                       # the truncation
ax.set_ylabel("Efficiency")                    # units quietly gone
ax.set_xlabel("Month")
ax.set_title("Efficiency SURGES in Q2!")       # editorial title
plt.show()












(a) Same six data points, twice.











(b)







Figure 1



Version A: the y-axis spans 0–100%, and the truthful story is essentially flat — a stable motor drifting up half a percent. Version B: the y-axis spans 94.0–94.9%, the line is thick and red, the title editorializes, the units label has quietly vanished — and the visual story is dramatic improvement. Same data. Neither plot contains a false number. One of them is still a lie.
Axis truncation is the workhorse of misleading plots, but know the whole family: cherry-picked ranges (start the x-axis after the bad quarter), missing units, dual y-axes tuned to force a visual correlation, 3D bars that distort area. You need this skill twice over — as a maker (A2: your plots tell the truth, including choosing axis limits that represent the effect honestly) and as a reader (you will spend a career on the receiving end of Version B, in vendor datasheets, in pitch decks, in the news).






TipThink



Is a truncated axis always dishonest? Suppose the half-percent drift genuinely matters — a bearing wearing in, say. Zooming the axis to show it isn’t a lie; it’s the point. The honest move is zooming and saying so (“note: y-axis spans 94–95% to resolve the drift”). The dishonest move is zooming and letting the reader assume they’re seeing 0-to-100 drama. Honesty lives in the disclosure, not the axis limits — which is why A2 and A3 (provenance, stated context) are woven together.

title: Data in, data out — and honest plots
section: Look at raw data before you compute
text:
Look at raw data before you compute
Last habit, permanent: plot the raw data before processing it. Summary numbers — means, fits, five-number reductions — can be identical for datasets with wildly different shapes: a clean trend, a curve, a cloud with one outlier dragging everything. Thirty seconds of scatter-plotting catches what statistics conceal: the dead sensor that logged zeros for an hour, the unit change halfway through the file, the outlier that is either your discovery or your glitch. The computer computes; you look.

Find a plot in the wild — news article, ad, social media, product page — that you judge misleading, and bring it (screenshot or link, on your phone is fine) with two sentences on paper: what technique makes it misleading, and what an honest version would look like. Thursday’s plot clinic: each table makes one honest and one deliberately misleading plot of the same provided dataset, and the other tables have to catch the trick. Yes, we are teaching you to lie with plots, once, under supervision, so you can spot it forever.

title: Logic & edge cases
text: This week the code learns to make decisions — and you learn that edge cases, the places where decisions get made, are where specifications go to die.

title: Logic & edge cases
text:
Think First
Recall

Week 1, the robot sandwich: what happens to every question your instructions didn’t answer?
Week 3: what did fall_time(3.0) assume about the sign of the input? What should fall_time(-3.0) do?

Look Ahead

Is a negative flow rate an error, or just flow in the other direction?
Would you rather a program crash loudly or continue quietly with a bad value?

title: Logic & edge cases
text:
Booleans: questions with yes/no answers
A boolean is a value that is either True or False. Comparisons produce them:








The = vs == confusion causes real bugs weekly, worldwide, at every experience level. Read == as “is it equal?” — a question — and = as “gets” — a command.

title: Logic & edge cases
Logic & edge cases
section: Edge cases are specification questions wearing code costumes
text:
Edge cases are specification questions wearing code costumes
Here is the deepest idea this week. Consider a flow-rate input of -3.0 L/min. What should the pool-fill function do?

Crash with ValueError("flow rate must be positive")?
Return a negative fill time and let the caller deal with it?
Interpret it as draining and compute time-to-empty?

Python has no opinion. All three are two lines of code. The decision is engineering — it depends on what the program is for, who calls it, and what failure costs. This is exactly the week-1 lesson coming home: an edge case is a gap in the spec, and something will fill the gap. Either you decide, or the AI’s statistical average of the internet decides, or physics decides at runtime. Pick the first one.






Important



When you prompt an AI for a function, your spec should answer the edge questions explicitly: “raise a ValueError for non-positive flow rates.” Watch what happens when you don’t: the AI picks one of the three behaviors, confidently, without telling you which.

title: Logic & edge cases
text:
Defensive functions
The professional habit — a function that checks its own inputs and fails loudly and usefully:






Live cell — now abuse it: change the flow to -3.0 and run. That error message, loud and specific, is what your functions owe their callers.
raise stops the program with your message. Compare the debugging experience: ValueError: flow must be positive, got -3.0 versus a silent negative fill time propagating into a report your boss reads. Loud failure is a gift to your future self. (Recall week 2a: you will come to prefer the crash.)

title: Logic & edge cases
text:
Preview: while, the conditional loop
T = 90.0
minutes = 0
while T > 40:          # keep going as long as this is True
    T = T - 2.5        # coffee cools 2.5 degrees per minute (crude model)
    minutes = minutes + 1
print(minutes)
Read it as “repeat until the condition breaks.” Predict the printed value (how many 2.5° steps from 90 down to 40 or below?) — the answer settles at Tuesday’s tables, not here — then notice the danger: if the loop body never changes T, the condition never breaks and the program runs forever. Every while loop is a small specification exercise: what guarantees this ends?

For the battery_status function above, commit on paper to its output for these four inputs: 44, 45, 61, and -40. Two are ordinary; two are edges. For each edge, add one sentence: is the function’s behavior correct, and what would you change in the spec? Thursday’s vote is on -40 — a temperature a Colorado battery will actually see — and then the edge-case hunt: tables get each other’s week-3 functions and try to break them with hostile inputs. Bring your meanest test cases.

text: Tuesday you ran code. Today you learn to read it — which, in a course where AI handles production, is the load-bearing skill — and then we put the whole week-1 philosophy through one complete lap: spec → prompt → annotate → verify.

text:
The reading vocabulary
You already know enough Python to read most short engineering scripts. Here’s the honest inventory, plus two constructs you haven’t formally learned but will see in AI output long before we cover them:







You see
It means




x = 5
store 5 under the name x (“gets”, not “equals”)


print(x)
display the value of x


x ** 2, x / y
power, division


# text
note for humans; Python skips it


if condition:
preview (week 4): run the indented block only when the condition holds


for item in things:
preview (week 5): run the indented block once per item



You don’t need to write if or for yet. You need to recognize their shape — indentation marks the “inside” — so AI-generated code doesn’t look like hieroglyphics for the next two weeks.

title: Reading code & the full cycle
section: Tracing: running code in your head
text:
Tracing: running code in your head
To trace a program, be the computer: go top to bottom, one line at a time, keeping a little table of every variable’s current value.






(Runnable — after your trace. The print line is added so the machine can confirm your paper.)






NoteClick to see the trace





After line 1: a = 2. After line 2: a = 2, b = 5. After line 3: a = 20, b = 5 (note: b doesn’t move — it stored a value, not a relationship). After line 4: c = 25.
If you got c = 25, you can trace. If you got c = 7, you read = as algebra again — go re-run the week-2a mental patch.



Tracing is slow and that’s fine. It’s a verification instrument, not a way of life: you deploy it on the lines you don’t trust.

title: Reading code & the full cycle
text:
The annotation discipline
When an AI hands you code, you will annotate it: a comment on every line or logical block, in your own words, saying what it does and why it’s there. Two rules, permanent for the semester:






Important



Rule 1: A line you cannot annotate is a line you do not understand, and a line you do not understand does not enter your program. Investigate it or delete it.
Rule 2: Annotate the why, not just the what. # convert to liters beats # multiply by 1000 — the first survives a bug hunt, the second is just the code again, slower.


This feels tedious in week 2. It is also, quietly, your entire preparation for the final defense — a project annotated as it grows is a project you can explain under examination. Students who skip this discipline meet it again in week 14, at the worst possible time.

title: Reading code & the full cycle
section: One full lap: the pool problem
text:
One full lap: the pool problem
The problem: How long will it take to fill a backyard swimming pool with a garden hose?
Step 1 — Specification. Before any AI is involved, decisions: Inputs — pool length, width, depth (m), hose flow rate (L/min). Output — fill time in hours, displayed with units. Assumptions — rectangular pool, constant flow, starts empty, no evaporation or splashing (fine at this timescale). Edge cases — zero or negative flow rate should stop with a clear error, not divide by zero or report a negative time.
Step 2 — The prompt. Notice how the spec practically is the prompt:

Write a short Python script that computes the time to fill a rectangular pool. Inputs as variables: length, width, depth in meters, and flow rate in liters per minute. Convert consistently, output the fill time in hours with a printed sentence including units. Comment each step.

Step 3 — Annotate what comes back. Suppose the AI returns:






The two arrow-comments are annotation doing its real job: flagging the hinges — the lines where a silent error would live.
Step 4 — Verify. Hand estimate: volume is \(8 \times 4 \times 1.5 = 48\) m³ = 48,000 L. At ~10 L/min that’s ~4,800 min ≈ 80 hours. Program says 84.2. Agreement — trust earned. Unit check: trace the units through each line (they cancel to hours — do it). Edge case: set flow = 0 and predict before running what happens.


About 3.5 days of continuous garden hose. Verification sometimes delivers engineering judgment for free: the answer is “rent a water truck.”

title: Reading code & the full cycle
section: When the AI gets it plausibly wrong
text:
When the AI gets it plausibly wrong
Same prompt, different day, and the returned code contains:
volume_L = volume_m3 * 100    # convert cubic meters to liters
It runs. It plots nothing suspicious. It reports a fill time of 8.4 hours — brisk, believable, wrong by a factor of ten. The comment even asserts the conversion confidently. Only two things catch this: the hand estimate (80 ≠ 8.4) and the annotation pass (is 1 m³ really 100 L? A cube 10 dm on a side holds 10 × 10 × 10 = 1000 L). Nothing about running the program catches it. This is the “confident, invisibly wrong” failure mode from week 1, in the wild — and you just watched two cheap habits kill it.

Below is an AI-generated script with three planted flaws: one syntax error (won’t run), one logic error (runs, obviously wrong), and one silent error (runs, plausibly wrong). On paper: annotate every line, name all three flaws, and state what the correct fill time should be. Do not run it first — Thursday’s opening vote is which line hides the silent one, and the fun is finding it by reading.
flow = 9.5            # hose flow rate, liters per minute
length = 8            # m
width = 4             # m
depth = 1.5           # m

volume = length * width * width   # pool volume, m^3
volume_liters = volume * 1000     # convert m^3 to liters
minutes = volume_liters / flow    # minutes to fill
hours = minutes * 60              # convert minutes to hours
print("Fill time:", hours "hours")

title: What does an LLM actually do?
text: You will use AI constantly in this course, so we are going to spend one lesson opening the hood. Not because you need to build one — you need to build a mental model of one, so its behavior stops being magic and starts being predictable. Engineers don’t use instruments they don’t understand the failure modes of.
crumbs: What does an LLM actually do?

title: What does an LLM actually do?
text:
Think First
Recall

Your phone’s keyboard suggests the next word as you type. How do you think it decides what to suggest?
Have you ever confidently “remembered” something that turned out to be wrong — a fact you’d have bet money on? What did that feel like from the inside?

Look Ahead

If two students give an AI the exact same prompt, will they get the exact same code back?
Why might an AI be better at writing code than at doing arithmetic?

title: What does an LLM actually do?
text:
The one-sentence version
A large language model does one thing:

Given some text, predict a plausible next small chunk of text. Then do it again. And again.

That’s it. That is the entire mechanism. Everything else — the code-writing, the explanations, the apparent reasoning — emerges from doing that one thing extremely well, at enormous scale.


The “small chunks” are called tokens — usually a word or piece of a word. thermal might be one token; thermodynamics might be three.
The model learned to do this by, in effect, reading a colossal amount of text — books, articles, documentation, and critically for us, billions of lines of code — and adjusting billions of internal numerical knobs until its next-chunk predictions got very good. When you prompt it, you’re providing the start of a text, and it continues that text one chunk at a time, each new chunk chosen based on everything that came before.
crumbs: What does an LLM actually do?

title: What does an LLM actually do?
text:
Three consequences you must internalize
Everything strange about LLM behavior falls out of that mechanism. Three consequences matter for this course.

1. It’s plausibility, not truth
The model produces text that is statistically likely to follow your prompt — text shaped like a correct answer. Usually, the most plausible continuation of an engineering question is the correct answer, which is why these tools are so useful. But when the model doesn’t “know,” it does not stop and say so. It keeps generating plausible text — a function name that sounds real but isn’t, a formula with one term quietly wrong, a citation to a paper that doesn’t exist. This is often called hallucination, and the dangerous part is the fluency: wrong answers arrive in the same confident voice as right ones.






Important



There is no tone-of-voice difference between an LLM being right and an LLM being wrong. Your verification habits are the only alarm system you get.




2. Same prompt, different answers
Prediction produces a menu of plausible next chunks, each with a probability — and by design, the model doesn’t always pick the single most likely one. A bit of controlled randomness in the choice makes output more varied and, usually, better. Run the same prompt twice and the choices fork somewhere, and once forked, the two continuations keep diverging.
This is why, on Thursday, thirty tables prompting for the same task will produce thirty different programs — different variable names, different structures, sometimes different algorithms, occasionally different answers. In this course that divergence isn’t a nuisance; it’s the curriculum. “Why did your table’s code come out different from ours, and which one is right?” is the most instructive question we will ask all semester.


3. Your specification is the steering wheel
The model fills every gap in your prompt with a plausible assumption — plausible on average across everything it has read, not plausible for your specific problem. Ask for “a program to compute the trajectory of a projectile” and you’ll get something — but did it include air resistance? What launch angle convention? Degrees or radians? SI units? You didn’t say, so it guessed.
This is the punchline of the whole week: specification (Tuesday’s lesson) is precisely the skill that controls an LLM. A vague prompt doesn’t get you a wrong answer; it gets you a correct answer to a question you didn’t quite ask — which is worse, because it looks right.
crumbs: What does an LLM actually do?

title: What does an LLM actually do?
section: Why is it so good at code, anyway?
text:
Why is it so good at code, anyway?
Two reasons, one obvious, one useful to know.
The obvious one: the training data included billions of lines of code, much of it from working software, so the statistical patterns of correct code run deep.
The useful one: code is checkable in a way prose isn’t. An essay can be subtly wrong forever; a program can be run. It either produces \(0.78\) s for the falling wrench or it doesn’t. This is great news for engineers — it means the verification tools you’ll build in this course have real teeth. It’s also why we can hand production to the AI with a straight face: not because the AI is trustworthy, but because code is auditable and you’re going to learn to audit it.


Contrast: LLMs are historically mediocre at arithmetic — predicting the text-shape of a calculation is not the same as calculating. Modern tools patch this by letting the model write and run actual code for the math. Worth remembering: even the AI doesn’t trust itself with arithmetic.
crumbs: What does an LLM actually do?

title: What does an LLM actually do?
text:
The stance of this course
Here’s the relationship we’re building toward, stated plainly:
The LLM is your extremely fast, extremely well-read, occasionally overconfident junior collaborator. You are the engineer of record. You direct it (specification), you check its work (verification), and you sign your name to the result. That’s not a course rule invented to keep you honest — it is exactly the arrangement practicing engineers describe with these tools, and companies are notably uninterested in hiring people who can’t play the senior role in it.
What this course will never ask you to do is pretend the AI doesn’t exist. What it will constantly ask you to do is prove you were in charge: show your specification, annotate what came back, demonstrate your verification, and — at the end of the semester — explain what is actually going on inside a project with your name on it, on paper, with no AI in the room.






TipThink



People sometimes describe an LLM as “autocomplete on steroids.” Having read this lesson: in what sense is that fair, and in what sense does it undersell what’s happening? Hold that tension — it’s the beginning of a calibrated relationship with the tool, which is worth more than either hype or dismissal.



Commit, on paper, to answers to both of these — Thursday’s opening votes:

Two students give an LLM the identical prompt for a projectile program. Predict: (a) identical code, (b) different code, same numerical answers, (c) different code, possibly different answers. Write one sentence defending your pick.
The LLM hands you a projectile program and it runs without any errors, and produces a nice plot. List every distinct reason you can think of that its output might still be wrong. (Thursday we’ll pool the class list. It’s longer than you think.)

title: Getting going in your language
text:
A few recommendations, if you want them. The honest headline: you can do this entire course in Google Colab — nothing to install, works on any machine including a locked-down Chromebook, and it’s where the lessons and activities assume you are. Start there; most of you can stay there.
But at some point — the design project is a natural moment — running Python on your own machine starts paying off: your files live where you can see them, nothing depends on a wifi connection, and you get a real editor. This page is for that moment. MATLAB has some special steps because we have a license through the school, though overall its installation is probably the easiest of everything here.

title: Getting going in your language
text:
Level 0: Google Colab (where everyone starts)
Go to colab.research.google.com, sign in with your university Google account, click New notebook. That’s the entire installation. Python runs on Google’s computers; NumPy, matplotlib, and pandas are pre-installed; your notebooks live in your Google Drive. The one thing to learn early is file handling — where an uploaded CSV goes and why it vanishes when the session ends — which is exactly what Base Camp’s BC0 session covers.

title: Getting going in your language
text:
Level 1: Python on your machine
There are multiple avenues here, and if you are confident enough to find your own way (e.g., with pip and venv), I believe in you.
My recommendation is to install miniconda — NOT the full Anaconda, which you can find nearby if you really want to, but I’m not linking it. Anaconda is attractive: everything you’d ever need in one install. Also a lot you’ll never need, plus a sluggish navigator that insists on cross-checking every package each time you update. I grew to hate it and “downgraded” to miniconda: no navigator, way fewer packages, no regrets.
For the editor, I recommend VS Code — it supports Jupyter notebooks (so your Colab habits transfer directly), has an integrated terminal, and its GitHub integration will matter to anyone who takes the version-control Side Quest. Install VS Code, then its Python and Jupyter extensions (VS Code will offer them the first time you open a .py or .ipynb file).

Package management
Miniconda starts with essentially no packages, so you’ll install what you need from the command line. NumPy, matplotlib, and pandas cover this course; this page has the instructions. Note that miniconda still uses conda as the command.


pip is another package-management option — really not that different from conda. If you have reason to go that way, do it; plenty of tutorials around.






TipAlso worth installing



Seaborn sits on top of matplotlib and is beautiful. SciPy is a deep toolbox of numerical routines — and unlike some later courses that make you build tools from fundamentals, nothing in this course forbids it: our concern is whether you can specify and verify, not whether you hand-rolled the algorithm. For the ML-taster Side Quest, scikit-learn is what we’ll reach for.








NotePython “environments” (optional reading)





Serious programmers give each project its own isolated “environment” with its own package versions, because packages sometimes conflict (the classic: some ML libraries lag behind the newest NumPy). For this course, working entirely in the base environment is fine. If you want the habit early: conda create --name mcen1030, then conda activate mcen1030, then conda install numpy installs into just that environment. Note you install per-environment — three environments can mean NumPy installed three times, and that’s normal.

title: Getting going in your language
text:
Level 2: MATLAB (week 11 and beyond)
MATLAB is the easiest install of everything on this page. As a CU student you have free access: create a MathWorks account with your CU email — instructions are here, under the student “How to get it.”
Once your account is tied to the school’s license, you can install desktop MATLAB or use MATLAB Online in the browser — students have used both, and you can hop back and forth. I like the immediacy of a local install and it runs a bit faster; Online gives you your code from any computer. For this course’s purposes (week 11’s translation work and HW 9), MATLAB Online is entirely sufficient — treat it as MATLAB’s Colab.
Basic MATLAB is all this course needs; no toolboxes required. If you’re going on in the department, toolboxes like Simulink (used in System Dynamics) can be added anytime, so there’s no need to decide now.
The MathWorks “MATLAB Onramp” tutorial — find it under Online Training at matlab.mathworks.com — is genuinely good, takes about two hours, and is the recommended pre-read for week 11 if you want a head start.

title: Getting going in your language
section: Which level do I need, and when?
text:
Which level do I need, and when?
Weeks 1–10: Level 0 is enough, full stop — and the lesson pages themselves run Python in your browser for quick experiments, which is Level −1. The project (weeks 11–14): Level 0 still works, but Level 1 makes multi-file work and file management dramatically saner, and teams that take the Git Side Quest will want it. Week 11 / HW 9: Level 2, and MATLAB Online is fine. If your machine fights you at any point: bring it to a Monday session — installation archaeology is a group sport.

title: Homework
text:
Homework in this course does not ask you to hand in code for grading. It asks you to hand in engineering: the specification you designed, the AI-produced code you audited, the verification you ran, and the report you’d stand behind. Every set uses the same four-step submission, which is the course’s whole philosophy in miniature:
Step 1 — Specify. Design the problem specification: inputs, outputs, what happens in the middle, edge cases decided. Then write the actual prompt you gave the LLM. (These are graded on completeness, not on matching some secret official spec — there isn’t one.)
Step 2 — Annotate. The code that came back, with every line or block annotated in your own words — the why, not just the what. A line you can’t annotate is a line you delete or investigate.
Step 3 — Verify. Your tests and their results: the hand estimate, the edge cases exercised, the intuition checks — including any that failed and what you did about it. A verification section with no failures in it all semester is, statistically, a verification section that isn’t looking.
Step 4 — Report. A short published result (a Quarto page or PDF): the problem, the method, the answer, an honest plot where relevant, and the provenance someone would need to rerun you.
One logistical note: the lesson pages run Python in your browser for quick experiments, but homework is not browser work — do it in Colab or on your own machine (see getting going), where files live somewhere findable, persist between sessions, and can be handed to a teammate. Real work needs a real file system; part of what homework trains is exactly that management.
Each set names the standards it feeds. AI use is expected throughout; what’s yours — and what’s graded — is steps 1, 3, and 4, and the annotation quality in step 2. title: HW 8 · The parking lot
text: An autonomous shuttle enters a parking structure: a grid of aisles, some fraction of spots occupied, no map of which. At each intersection it randomly turns left, turns right, or continues straight; it takes the first open spot it passes. The fleet operator’s question: how does average time-to-park grow as the structure fills up — and at what occupancy does random search stop being acceptable?

title: HW 8 · The parking lot
text: An autonomous shuttle enters a parking structure: a grid of aisles, some fraction of spots occupied, no map of which. At each intersection it randomly turns left, turns right, or continues straight; it takes the first open spot it passes. The fleet operator’s question: how does average time-to-park grow as the structure fills up — and at what occupancy does random search stop being acceptable?

title: HW 8 · The parking lot
text:
The task
This is your first Monte Carlo simulation — marching a system forward in time (week 9) where the rate law is replaced by dice. One run of your simulation answers nothing: it’s one lucky or unlucky shuttle. The instrument is many runs, averaged — which is a parameter sweep (week 5) where the swept parameter is the random seed, wrapped in another sweep over occupancy. Every tool you own, one machine.
Your Step 1 spec has real design authority here, and must decide (with reasons): the grid size and geometry; how occupancy is laid out (uniform? clustered near the entrance, like reality?); what happens at walls; what “time” means (intersections visited is fine); how many runs per occupancy makes the average trustworthy — and how you’d check that number is enough (hint: does the answer move if you double it? — that’s dt-halving’s sibling).

title: HW 8 · The parking lot
text:
Your submission
Steps 1–4. Step 3: verify the machinery on a case with a known answer — a lot with exactly one open spot in a 1×N aisle has a computable expectation; or at minimum, the limiting sanity checks (0% full → park almost immediately; 100% full → your spec’s decided behavior, which had better not be an infinite loop). Step 4: the curve — mean time-to-park vs. occupancy with honest spread shown (not just the mean — the operator cares about bad days) — your recommended occupancy threshold, and the S2 paragraph: three ways your model is a lie about real parking lots, and which lie you’d fix first.
Optional bonus: give the shuttle one non-random strategy (e.g., prefer straight; or bias away from recently-visited aisles) and show the curve shift. One strategy, honestly compared, is worth more than five vibes-compared.

title: HW 6 · Track the station
text: Build the instrument from week 1’s demo yourself: a logger that samples the International Space Station’s position over at least 20 minutes, saves the data with full provenance, and reports the ground track and the station’s speed.

title: HW 6 · Track the station
text: Build the instrument from week 1’s demo yourself: a logger that samples the International Space Station’s position over at least 20 minutes, saves the data with full provenance, and reports the ground track and the station’s speed.

title: HW 6 · Track the station
text:
The task
The keyless API from the week-8 reading (api.wheretheiss.at) answers with JSON: timestamp, latitude, longitude, altitude, velocity. Your program: request politely on a schedule (the reading’s time.sleep sermon applies — your spec states your sampling interval and why), accumulate rows, and write a CSV whose header block records the provenance: the URL, when the run started and ended, the interval, and who ran it — written by the program itself. Let the computer keep the receipts.
Then the analysis: plot the ground track (longitude vs. latitude — and your spec must decide what to do if the track crosses the ±180° longitude seam mid-run, because sometimes it will); and compute average speed two ways — as reported by the API’s velocity field, and independently from your own consecutive positions and timestamps (great-circle distance over elapsed time).

title: HW 6 · Track the station
text:
Your submission
Steps 1–4. Step 3’s centerpiece is the two-way speed comparison — they won’t match exactly (your spec should predict why not before you run: sampling interval, altitude, rounding), and the A1 anchor is the 90-minute-orbit sanity check from the reading. Step 4: the track plot, both speeds with the discrepancy honestly stated, and the provenance block reproduced — a stranger must be able to rerun you from Step 4 alone.
Colab note: a 20-minute logging run means a 20-minute open notebook. Plan your run; the deliverable includes the run’s actual timestamps, so “I’ll fake shorter” is self-reporting.

title: HW 4 · The siren
text:
A stationary microphone recorded an emergency vehicle driving past on a straight road. From the recording, we extracted apparent frequency versus time — that file is yours. Determine the vehicle’s speed (and say what else about its motion you can and cannot determine from this data).
Data: siren_frequency.csv — columns time_s, frequency_Hz. Real-world flavor included: the data is noisy.

title: HW 4 · The siren
text:
A stationary microphone recorded an emergency vehicle driving past on a straight road. From the recording, we extracted apparent frequency versus time — that file is yours. Determine the vehicle’s speed (and say what else about its motion you can and cannot determine from this data).
Data: siren_frequency.csv — columns time_s, frequency_Hz. Real-world flavor included: the data is noisy.

title: HW 4 · The siren
text:
Background
For a source moving at speed \(U\) along a straight line with closest-approach distance \(y_0\) from the observer, emitting true frequency \(f_0\), the observed frequency is
\[f_{obs}(t) = \frac{f_0}{1 - \dfrac{U}{c}\cos\theta(t)}, \qquad \cos\theta(t) = \frac{-U\,(t - t_{pass})}{\sqrt{U^2 (t-t_{pass})^2 + y_0^2}}\]
where \(c = 343\) m/s and \(t_{pass}\) is the moment of closest approach. Note the honest inventory of unknowns: \(U\), \(f_0\), \(y_0\), \(t_{pass}\) — you know none of them. The data knows all of them.

title: HW 4 · The siren
section: The idea that makes this solvable
text:
The idea that makes this solvable
There is no algebra that inverts noisy data into \(U\). But you own a machine for exactly this: the parameter sweep as a search. Build the model function; guess parameters; compute how badly the model’s curve misses the data (one honest number — the spec decision is which number); sweep the guesses; the best fit is your answer. This is the week-1 promise — “solving the unsolvable numerically” — cashed in full, and it is secretly how half of experimental engineering works.
Hints your spec should chew on: two of the four unknowns can be read nearly off the plot before any sweeping (which two? plot the data first — always). That collapses a hopeless 4-D search into a manageable one.

title: HW 4 · The siren
text:
Your submission
Steps 1–4. Step 3 must include an A1 estimate that requires no fitting at all: the far-approach and far-recede frequencies bound \(f_0\) and give a direct first estimate of \(U\) (how?) — your sweep answer must agree with it or one of them is wrong. Step 4’s plot: data and best-fit curve together, honestly labeled, with your recovered parameters and a sentence on which parameter the fit is least certain about and how you can tell.

text:
The data
A Python dictionary stores values under names (you met the idea in week 8’s reading as JSON’s cousin; here it is early, in its natural habitat):
materials = {
    "aluminum_6061": {"k_W_mK": 167, "rho_kg_m3": 2700, "c_J_kgK":  896},
    "copper":        {"k_W_mK": 401, "rho_kg_m3": 8960, "c_J_kgK":  385},
    "steel_1045":    {"k_W_mK": 49.8,"rho_kg_m3": 7870, "c_J_kgK":  486},
    "pine":          {"k_W_mK": 0.12,"rho_kg_m3":  510, "c_J_kgK": 2300},

title: HW 2 · The materials librarian
text:
The task
A function get_property(material, prop) that returns the value — and behaves deliberately at the edges: material not in the library? Property misspelled? "Aluminum 6061" with a capital letter and a space? Each of those is a Step-1 decision (crash loudly with a useful message? attempt to normalize the name? suggest near-matches?), and your spec must make it, with one sentence of reasoning each.

title: HW 2 · The materials librarian
text:
Your submission
Step 1 — spec + prompt, edges decided. Step 2 — annotated code. Step 3 — verify: one lookup checked against your source by hand; every edge case from your spec exercised, with the actual messages shown. Step 4 — a half-page “library card”: the materials, the sources, how to call it, what it does when abused. Keep the file — HW 7 imports it.

title: How your grade works
text:
Your grade is built from exactly two ingredients, and understanding them takes five minutes:
There are no points, no weighted averages, no partial credit, and no curve. There is also no penalty for struggling early — read on.

title: How your grade works
text:
Standards: Met or Not Yet
Every standard gets multiple opportunities across the semester (checkpoints, in-class work, the project, the defense — the schedule shows where each appears). The marking rules:

Convergent standards (the ones with checkable right answers) require two successful demonstrations, on different occasions. One success might be a fluke or a neighbor; two is a skill.
Divergent standards (open-ended; judged, not checked) require one demonstration at “Meets” quality, with the right to revise and resubmit once per artifact.
“Not Yet” means not yet. A standard missed in week 4 and demonstrated in week 11 is Met, full stop, no discount. Your grade records where you ended up, because that’s what learning a skill means. (The one bound: reassessment happens at the scheduled reappearances of each standard, plus token-purchased retries — see Tokens. It is not unlimited-on-demand, because your graders are mortal.)

title: How your grade works
text:
Checkpoints
Four Tuesdays — weeks 4, 6, 8, and 10 — open with a checkpoint: about twenty minutes, individual, on paper, no AI, no notes. Each checkpoint assesses a few convergent standards and re-offers items from earlier checkpoints — which is what makes “Not Yet means not yet” a mechanism rather than a slogan. The rule that gives the whole system its spine: at least one of a convergent standard’s two demonstrations must be in-class — at a checkpoint or on the defense.
Checkpoints are also where a small amount of unaided writing lives: expect to produce a short function by hand from a given spec — five lines or so, no AI in the room. Why, in a course that delegates production? Because verification requires a minimum writing fluency: you cannot audit a language you can’t produce a sentence in. Checkpoint items are marked Met / Not Yet per standard like everything else; there is no checkpoint “score,” and a rough checkpoint costs you nothing that the re-offers can’t repair. (Rough checkpoints are also how Base Camp invitations happen — see Base Camp — which is a resource, not a consequence.)

title: How your grade works
text:
Engagement credits: protecting the process
This course runs on committed preparation and in-room collaboration — the opening votes, the table arguments, the critiques. Those can’t be graded on correctness without poisoning them (nobody argues honestly at a table where wrong answers cost points). So they’re credited for good-faith completion instead:

Rules of the road: credits are checked for committed good-faith work — a wrong answer with reasoning earns full credit; a blank or a transparently uncommitted scribble earns none. Credits are earned in the room (that’s the point), with tokens as the illness/life valve. And note the arithmetic below is deliberately forgiving: an A requires 40 of ~50, so you can fully miss about a fifth of everything and feel no effect.


Why credits at all? Because without them, the rational move is to skip the preparation and coast on the tables’ work — and this course is the tables. Credits make the preparation count without making it a quiz. (Design borrowed from Robert Talbert’s pairing of engagement credits with standards-based grading.)

Project-period credits are individual
The 8 credits of the project period (pin-ups #1 and #2, the mock defense) are awarded per person, informed by teammate evaluation — two short, description-based evaluations, one formative in week 13 and one summative in finals week. The default outcome is nothing: ordinary teams keep ordinary credits. The instrument exists for the teammate no one can describe. Full mechanics, including exactly what the form asks and why it asks for descriptions rather than ratings, on the peer evaluation page.

title: How your grade works
text:
Tokens
Everyone starts the semester with 3 tokens. Spend one for: a 48-hour deadline extension; an excused activity (the engagement credits without attending — illness, interviews, life); or one extra reassessment of a convergent standard outside its scheduled windows. No questions asked, no documentation required — that’s what the tokens are for. Unspent tokens convert to 1 engagement credit each at semester’s end, so hoarding isn’t punished.

title: How your grade works
text:
The grade table
Your letter grade is the highest row where you meet every requirement in that row:
