Plus: meet all of your row and at least one requirement of the row above → attach a plus (e.g., B+). Minus: exactly one requirement falls short of your row, and it lands in the row directly below → you get the higher grade with a minus rather than dropping a full letter. F is reserved for missing the D row.
Why P5 gates the A and B rows: P5 — holding your whole project in your head — is what the defense measures, and it’s the standard that certifies all the others were yours. An A in a course about directing and auditing computation, held by someone who can’t explain their own project, would be a false statement. We don’t issue those.

title: How your grade works
text:
Three worked examples
Maya — the straightforward case. Meets 14 standards including P5 (only S4 still Not Yet after the project), earns 43 engagement credits, spends one token on an extension during a brutal midterm week. Check the A row: 14 ≥ 14 ✓, P5 ✓, 43 ≥ 40 ✓. Grade: A. Her two unspent tokens add 2 credits (45), which changes nothing — comfort, not currency.
Dev — the slow start (read this one if you’re nervous). Bombs the first checkpoint: P1 and P4 both Not Yet in week 4, and it feels catastrophic. It isn’t — both standards are re-offered at the week-6 and week-8 checkpoints, and he’s demonstrated each twice by mid-semester. He finishes with 12 standards Met including P5 (S2 and A3 fell short on the project report; his revision closed A3 but not S2, and F1 never came together), and 41 engagement credits, because he did the work all semester even while the checkpoints were rough. B row: 12 ≥ 12 ✓, P5 ✓, 41 ≥ 32 ✓ → at least a B. Plus check: does he meet ≥ 1 requirement of the A row? His 41 credits clear the A row’s 40 ✓. Grade: B+. Note what his early disasters cost him in the final calculation: nothing. The grade records where he ended up.
Priya — the ghost (read this one if you’re planning to skip class). Brilliant, and knows it: 13 standards Met including P5, some on first attempt. But she treats the room as optional — skips the readings’ commitments, misses most Thursdays — and finishes with 22 engagement credits, having spent no tokens (which convert: 22 + 3 = 25). B row: standards ✓ ✓, but 25 < 32 ✗. C row: 13 ≥ 10 ✓, 25 ≥ 24 ✓ → at least a C. Plus check: she meets two B-row requirements (standards, P5) → Grade: C+. Is that harsh for someone with 13 standards? It’s the design working as stated: this course certifies engineers who can work the process — prepare, commit, argue, critique — because that’s the half of the job the standards can’t see. The fix was never talent; it was showing up. (And the near-miss sting is intentional: at 32 credits — ten more Thursdays of just participating — she’s a B+.)

title: How your grade works
text:
The philosophy, in one paragraph
Standards answer “can you do the thing?” Engagement credits answer “did you do the work?” A course grade should require both, because your degree asserts both. And nothing in this system rewards being right early — only being right eventually, which is the only kind of right that engineering careers are made of. Struggle freely. It’s priced in.






Note



Logistics: your current standards ledger and credit count live on Canvas, updated weekly. Arithmetic disputes are welcome and boring (bring them anytime); judgment disputes on divergent standards go through the revise-and-resubmit channel, which exists precisely for that conversation.

title: Mock defenses
text: Standards in play: P5, and everything under it · You’ll need: your three least-wanted questions; your project’s file map, printed.

title: Mock defenses
text:
The format
Tables run the real exam format on each other: ten minutes as examinee, ten as examiner, rotate until everyone has done both. Examiners work from the provided question bank (all five species: Trace, Justify, Predict, Audit, Verify) plus the examinee’s own submitted least-wanted questions — yes, we collected them for exactly this.

title: Mock defenses
text:
The rules of engagement
Examinee: answer from the printed file map and your head, exactly like finals — no laptop, no scrolling. Examiner: your job is calibrated difficulty — follow up on vague answers (“which file, specifically?”), and when an answer is solid, say so and move on. Grading the mock: nobody. Learning from it: everybody.

title: Mock defenses
text:
The debrief
Last fifteen minutes, tables inward: where did answers go vague? Those are your study assignments for the next four days, delivered with more precision than any review session could manage. Write them down before you leave — the mock defense’s entire value is the list you walk out holding.
Reminder: project-period credits are individual and peer-informed (details); evaluation #2 opens in finals week.
Deliverable (2 EC): participation in both chairs + your written where-I-went-vague list (for your eyes; checked for existence, never read).

title: Pin-up #1: specs & verification plans
text: Standards in play: S2, A3, A4, P5 · You’ll need: your spec (evolved from spec zero) and your verification plan, in presentable form.

title: Pin-up #1: specs & verification plans
text:
The format
Work goes up — screens outward or printed — before major code exists, because today the thinking is what’s on review. Tables rotate in two shifts (half present, half review, swap), ~8 minutes per station.

title: Pin-up #1: specs & verification plans
text:
The review questions
Reviewers work from the card (provided): Is the spec complete — inputs, outputs, edge cases decided? What’s assumed, and is the assumption list honest (S2)? What’s the verification plan — how will they know it works, concretely, with what hand-checkable case (A1)? What’s the riskiest unknown, and is it scheduled first or being avoided?

title: Pin-up #1: specs & verification plans
text:
Why now
A spec hole found today costs a conversation. The same hole found in week 14 costs your weekend and possibly your defense. Pin-up #1 exists to make the cheap version happen — so reviewers: the kindest thing you can do is be thorough. Etiquette in force: questions beat verdicts; one specific working-thing named per review.
Deliverable (3 EC): your station materials + the review cards your team wrote for others (quality assessed) + your one-paragraph “what we’re changing because of today,” due Monday.

title: Model critique
text: Standards seeded: S2, S3, S4 · You’ll need: your damped-oscillator commitments; your table’s week-9 model and its assumptions audit.

title: Model critique
text:
Opening vote
Damping doubles — what happens to the motion? Commit → vote → argue → revote. We settle it the S4 way: a live sweep over the damping coefficient, five futures on one plot. (Then the deeper cut, discussed: at what damping does it stop oscillating at all? Your dynamics course will name this moment; today you get to see it first.)

title: Model critique
text:
The critique
The main event, and the first formal rehearsal of pin-up culture. Tables exchange week-9 models with their assumption audits and review: Is the audit honest — what’s excluded that isn’t listed? Which of the three failure modes (numerical / physical / extrapolation) is nearest for this model, and what specifically would trigger it? Is there dt-halving evidence, or vibes? Written findings, critique etiquette in force: questions beat verdicts, and one specific thing-that-works named per review.

title: Model critique
text:
The response
Reviews return home. Each table gets ten minutes to respond in writing — accept, rebut, or amend the audit — engineering peer review in miniature. Findings and responses both turn in; both are assessed for critique quality, because giving good review is a standard-adjacent skill you’ll use forever.
Deliverable (3 EC): your table’s written critique of the received model + your written response to the critique you received.

title: Data acquisition lab
text: Standards seeded: F1, F2, A3 · You’ll need: your sketched weather JSON; a phone with Phyphox installed (one per table minimum); stairwell-compatible footwear.

title: Data acquisition lab
text:
Opening reveal
We query a real weather API from the front and put the actual JSON next to the class’s sketches. The gaps are the lesson: the timestamp nobody could interpret, the wind units nobody stated, the nesting nobody predicted. Rule extracted: never guess a shape — print it, then navigate it.

title: Data acquisition lab
text:
The stairwell
The main event. Phyphox recording, phone in pocket, one flight of stairs, walk normally. Export the CSV, load it with week-7 tools, plot acceleration vs. time — and find your own footsteps in the trace. Then the F2 questions: what’s the sampling rate (it’s discoverable from the data — how)? Which axis is vertical? Count the steps from the plot and check against the number your legs remember.

title: Data acquisition lab
text:
Provenance in practice
Before leaving: write the A3 record for your dataset — phone model, app settings, sampling rate, which pocket, which stairwell — as a header block in the file itself. Test: could another table re-run your analysis from the file alone? Swap files with a neighboring table and find out.
Deliverable (2 EC): your annotated acceleration plot with steps identified + the provenance header + the neighboring table’s verdict on rerunnability.

title: Plot clinic
text: Standards seeded: A2, F2 · You’ll need: your misleading plot from the wild; laptops.

title: Plot clinic
text:
Opening round
A gallery walk of the class’s found-in-the-wild plots (submitted at the door, displayed anonymously). Vote for the most deviously misleading; the finder of the winner explains the mechanism. There is a small prize and it is glory.

title: Plot clinic
text:
The clinic
Each table gets the same real dataset and produces two plots of it: one scrupulously honest, one deliberately misleading (technique of your choice — truncation, cherry-picked range, vanished units, editorial title). Plots go up anonymously, tables rotate: catch the trick in each pair, name the technique.

title: Plot clinic
text:
Debrief
The class builds the taxonomy on the board: every deception technique used today, plus its antidote. Closing question, discussed not voted: when is a zoomed axis honest? (Answer from the reading: when it’s disclosed. Now defend it against a skeptic at your table.)
Deliverable (2 EC): your table’s honest/misleading pair with a one-line disclosure statement for the honest one — the sentence you’d put in a real report.

title: The edge-case hunt
text: Standards seeded: P4, P1 · You’ll need: your battery_status commitments; your week-3 function.

title: The edge-case hunt
text:
Opening vote
battery_status(-40). Commit → vote → argue → revote. Then the real question, which has no single right answer and a genuinely interesting argument: what should it do at −40, and whose decision is that?

title: The edge-case hunt
text:
The hunt
Tables exchange week-3 functions and attack: zeros, negatives, absurd magnitudes, wrong-type inputs. Score a point per behavior that surprises the function’s author. Authors then patch: add the input checks the attack revealed, with loud, useful error messages.

title: The edge-case hunt
text:
The armistice
Each table reports its best kill. Class synthesizes the reusable checklist: the inputs that break engineering functions — zero, negative, boundary-exact, huge, empty. Photograph it; it’s your pre-flight checklist for every function you spec from now on.
Deliverable (2 EC): your patched function with its new defenses annotated, plus the attack log (what was tried, what broke).

title: The flaw hunt
text: Standards seeded: P4, A1, A4 · You’ll need: your annotated pool script from the reading (on paper, unexecuted).

title: The flaw hunt
text:
Opening vote
Which line hides the silent flaw? Commit → vote → argue → revote. Then, and only then, we run the script and let reality adjudicate — including watching the syntax error stop it cold before the interesting bugs even get a chance.

title: The flaw hunt
text:
Warm-up: assembly required
Ten minutes, before the hunt: each table gets the pool script’s lines on paper strips, scrambled. Reassemble a working order. Some lines have more than one valid position (which? why?) — and discovering that is your first taste of the difference between what a program must sequence and what it merely happens to.

title: The flaw hunt
text:
The hunt
Tables reconcile their annotations line by line: every line gets a why, every disagreement gets traced by hand. Then each table receives a second script (fresh flaws, same rules) and races: annotate, name all three flaw types, state the correct answer — before running.

title: The flaw hunt
text:
Debrief
The scoreboard truth we’re after: the hand estimate catches what running cannot. Tables report which flaw they found last — it’s almost always the silent one, and the reasons why are the lesson.
Deliverable (2 EC): the table’s annotated second script with the three flaws named and the corrected answer, initialed by every member.

title: Divergence & the ISS
text: Standards seeded: A4, A1 · You’ll need: your committed Bring-to-class answers; one laptop per table.

title: Divergence & the ISS
text:
Opening vote
Question 1 from the reading: identical prompts → identical code? Commit → vote → argue with your table → revote. Then we settle it live: every table sends the same projectile prompt to an LLM, and we tally what comes back.

title: Divergence & the ISS
text:
The class list
Question 2: the program ran and made a nice plot — why might it still be wrong? Tables pool their reasons, we build the master list on the board. This list gets photographed and becomes a course artifact; you will be checking your own work against it in week 14.

title: Divergence & the ISS
text:
The awesome part
Live, from the front: three lines of Python, and the International Space Station’s position, speed, and altitude appear. We sanity-check its speed against a 90-minute orbit — your first A1 in the wild. You’ll write this program yourself in week 8; today it’s here so you know where this course is going.
Deliverable (2 EC): your table’s contribution to the master list — at least three distinct failure reasons, on the provided card, team names on it.

title: The function forge
text: Standards seeded: P1, A4 · You’ll need: your Bring-to-class function spec with its hand-checked test case.

title: The function forge
text:
Opening vote
double(10) and the two results — which value prints? Commit → vote → argue → revote → run.

title: The function forge
text:
Warm-up: assembly required
Ten minutes: a working function, lines scrambled — def line, docstring, body, return, and two calls, in a pile. Reorder it. The arguments this forces (can the return come before the body? can a call precede the def?) are the structure of functions, learned by hand without writing a character.

title: The function forge
text:
The forge
The full A4 cycle, solo then table: prompt an LLM with your spec → annotate the function it returns → run it against your committed hand-check. Pass: you’ve earned a verified function (save it — week 5 sweeps it). Fail: the best moment of the day — is the AI’s code wrong, or was your hand arithmetic wrong? Your table adjudicates. Both happen every semester, in comparable numbers, which is itself the lesson.

title: The function forge
text:
Spec swap
Tables exchange one spec, sight unseen, and build from it. Where the built function surprises the spec’s author, the spec had a gap — the robot sandwich, now with consequences.
Deliverable (2 EC): your function, its annotation, and the test-case verdict (pass, or fail + diagnosis), submitted per person.

title: Sweep lab
text: Standards seeded: P2, S4, P1 · You’ll need: your accumulator trace; your sweep spec from the reading.

title: Sweep lab
text:
Opening vote
The accumulator: commit → vote → argue → revote → run. (If your table split between 56 and something else, trace it aloud together before the revote — the divergence is always the same line.)

title: Sweep lab
text:
The lab
Run your spec’d sweep for real: your verified week-3 function, your chosen range, 100 points, out to CSV. Then plot it (a preview of week 6) and answer the S4 question on paper: what does the shape tell you about the system? Steep where? Flat where? So what?

title: Sweep lab
text:
The amplifier demo
One table volunteers to sweep the week-2 pool function with the silent ×100 bug deliberately restored. We inspect the resulting CSV together: 100 rows, perfectly formatted, internally consistent, uniformly wrong. Nobody can find the bug from the output. That’s the point, and the P1 doctrine — verify once in isolation, then sweep — never needs defending again.
Deliverable (2 EC): your sweep CSV’s first ten rows + your plot + two sentences of shape interpretation.

title: Dataset triage
text: Standards seeded: P3, F2, A1 · You’ll need: your three by-eye answers from the 12-row miniature.

title: Dataset triage
text:
Opening vote
Question 3 from the miniature (which phase runs hotter?). Commit → vote → argue → revote. Then pandas answers the same question on the same 12 rows — and your paper answer is the acceptance test for your code, exactly the two-step from the reading.

title: Dataset triage
text:
The triage
Now the real file — motor_test_log.csv, 60,000 rows from the same (fictional but realistic) motor test. Tables get the engineering questions a supervisor would actually ask — How many over-temperature events? During which phase? Was the cooling fan compensating? — and answer them with filter/group/summarize, spot-checking one group by eye against raw rows.

title: Dataset triage
text:
The trap
One column in the file has a problem a spot-check catches and a blind mean() does not (you’ll know it when you find it — and the table that finds it first announces it). The lesson: head() and one plotted column before trusting any summary. Week 6’s “look first” habit, now at scale where looking is the only defense you have.
Deliverable (2 EC): answers to the supervisor questions + the spot-check evidence + what the trap was and how your table caught it.

title: Build-a-model lab
text: Standards seeded: S1, S3, A1 · You’ll need: your three hand-computed Euler steps; your over/undershoot commitment.

title: Build-a-model lab
text:
Opening vote
Too-big steps: above or below the true cooling curve? Commit → vote → argue → revote — then settle it with one plot, dt = 1 against dt = 25, projected from the front.

title: Build-a-model lab
text:
The lab
Each table draws a different system from the hat — draining tank, falling object with drag, charging capacitor, heating apartment, chemical mixing — each defined only by its rate law. Build the march: rate function (week 3), Euler loop (week 9 reading), plot (week 6). Required checkpoints, in order: three steps by hand first (A1); code matches hand steps; halve dt and compare (S3); shape interrogated against physical intuition — does the tank drain slower as it empties? should it?

title: Build-a-model lab
text:
The gallery
Every table’s system plots on the wall. The punchline hiding in plain sight: five different physical systems, and the shape keeps rhyming — the exponential approach to equilibrium is everywhere, because the rate-proportional-to-distance-from-equilibrium structure is everywhere. You’ve just discovered why one week of coffee generalizes to half of engineering.
Deliverable (2 EC): your model’s code + hand-step verification + the dt-halving evidence + one sentence on the shape’s physical story.

title: Project launch
text: Standards seeded: S2, A4, and the beginning of P5 · You’ll need: your MATLAB prediction; ambitions.

title: Project launch
text:
Opening vote
The MATLAB script: what does it display? Commit → vote → argue → revote → run. Note the flagged lines the class was least sure about — the vals(1) index is reliably among them, which is the off-by-one doctrine landing on schedule.

title: Project launch
text:
The launch
The project menu, presented with examples of strong past-style outcomes. Teams form (3–4; the roster is fixed today). Each team’s first hour of real work: choose from the menu (or pitch an original — bar: multi-file, verifiable), then draft specification zero: the problem in one paragraph, inputs and outputs, the three biggest unknowns, and — required — the first verification idea: how will you know any of it works?

title: Project launch
text:
The first desk crit

title: Base Camp
text:
Mondays are optional-session day in this course, all semester long. The first half of the semester, those Mondays are Base Camp: sessions built for one audience — people who are new to all of this. If week 2 is your first code ever, Base Camp is where your reps live. (The second half of the semester, Mondays become Side Quests — same room, same hour, different flavor.)
Let’s be precise about what this is, because the framing matters: Base Camp is not remedial. Nothing is wrong with you; something is simply true about you — you haven’t done this before — and that’s the single most fixable condition in engineering. Plenty of your classmates arrive with years of tinkering; you’re not behind them in ability, you’re behind them in hours, and hours are exactly what Mondays supply. The course was designed assuming zero prior experience. Base Camp is where that assumption gets honored with an instructor at your elbow.
The promises: no attendance is taken, nothing here affects your grade in any direction, and “I don’t understand variables yet” is not an admission here — it’s the entrance ticket. And a promise in the other direction too: these sessions are where we get to know each other. Office hours in every course you’ll ever take work better once you’ve learned that talking to your professor is just… talking. Mondays are the practice reps for that, too.
After each checkpoint, I may personally suggest a Monday session to a few people. If that’s you, hear it correctly — it is not a summons and not a judgment. It’s me doing arithmetic about hours, and pointing at where more of them live.
Time and room set by signup poll in week 1 — watch Canvas.

title: Base Camp
text:

Before any Python: the machine layer nobody teaches — Colab login, browsers vs. apps, where a downloaded file goes, folders, uploading to Colab, what “the cloud” means for your work. Then the second half, which pays off all semester: how to ask a question about code — the vocabulary (what do you call **, [], :?), and the professional question format: what I ran / what I expected / what I got instead. That format is simultaneously how you ask a TA, how you ask your table, and how you prompt an LLM — one skill, three doors. (No laptop yet? Come anyway; we’ll get you set up with campus options. The installing page covers the whole ladder, from Colab to your own machine.)
BC1 (Week 2) · First contact, slowly. The week 2 lesson again at half speed: cells, variables, running your first program, and learning to read error messages as information instead of accusation.
BC2 (Week 3) · The vocabulary drill. Reps on the core reading skills: trace variables by hand, predict outputs, read = as “gets.” Includes assembly problems — working code with its lines scrambled, yours to reorder — the missing rung between reading code and writing it.

Why this is harder than it looks
The grading page was written for humans, and humans fill gaps charitably. A program can’t. As you specify, you will run into questions the prose answers only if you read carefully — What if someone qualifies for a minus and a plus? Where the grading page is genuinely ambiguous, state your interpretation in the spec — that’s what engineers do with ambiguous requirements (right after asking, which you may also do in class).

title: HW 3 · The lightest beam
text: A cantilevered aluminum bracket of length \(L = 0.40\) m and width \(b = 30\) mm must carry a tip load \(P = 50\) N with tip deflection no more than 1.0 mm. Thickness is yours to choose — and every millimeter of thickness is money and mass. Find the thinnest acceptable beam.

title: HW 3 · The lightest beam
text:
Background
Tip deflection of a cantilever under a point tip load:
\[\delta = \frac{P L^3}{3 E I}, \qquad I = \frac{b\,t^3}{12}\]
with \(E = 69\) GPa for aluminum 6061 and \(t\) the thickness. Watch your units like a hawk — this problem is a unit-error honeypot, and that’s not an accident.

title: HW 3 · The lightest beam
text:
The task
This is the course’s marquee pattern, end to end: a verified function, swept.

A function tip_deflection(t, ...) — hand-checked in isolation first (P1): compute \(\delta\) for \(t = 20\) mm by hand and make the function agree before proceeding.
A sweep over thickness (P2): a sensible range, ~100 points, results to CSV.
The design answer, extracted from the sweep, plus a plot of \(\delta\) vs. \(t\) with the 1-mm limit drawn on.

title: HW 3 · The lightest beam
text:
Your submission
Steps 1–4 as always. In Step 3, your hand check is the P1 evidence — show the arithmetic. In Step 4, report the minimum thickness and answer the S4 question: the plot’s shape is dramatic (why, physically? — look at where \(t\) lives in the formula), so what does that shape tell a designer about the sensitivity of this decision, and about what a manufacturing tolerance of ±0.5 mm does to your margin?

title: HW 5 · Where the wind blows
text:
The task
This is pandas doing what pandas is for: reduce 60,000 numbers to one defensible decision.

Load, head(), and look first — a heatmap (or your preferred picture) of mean wind over the region before any optimizing. What structure do you see?
Reduce months → one mean per site (a groupby), then find the 10×10 square with the best mean wind. Your spec must decide: best by mean — or does the site’s consistency across months matter to a turbine business? (Both are computable; defending your choice is Step 4 material.)
A spot-check (A1): pick one site, verify its 6-month mean against the raw rows by eye.

title: HW 5 · Where the wind blows
text:
A warning, from experience
Regions like this contain visually dramatic features. The site your eye picks from the heatmap and the site the arithmetic picks are not guaranteed to be the same one — background gradients are sneaky, and eyeballs integrate badly. If they disagree, that disagreement goes in your report; it’s the most interesting thing you’ll find this week.

title: HW 5 · Where the wind blows
text:
Your submission
Steps 1–4. Step 4 is a one-page site recommendation: the winning square (corner coordinates), its mean wind, the runner-up and the margin, one honest map with the site drawn on, and your consistency argument. Write it for a boss who will spend real money on your answer.
Part B (short). Same skills, homier data: boulder_first_snow.csv holds 60 seasons of Boulder’s first-snowfall date. Report the average first-snow date, the earliest and latest on record, and one honest plot of the trend (is there one? don’t invent one). Two paragraphs, max.

title: HW 7 · The quench
text: A 1045-steel sphere, 5.0 cm diameter, leaves a furnace at 850 °C and is quenched in a large agitated water bath at 25 °C (convection coefficient \(h = 350\) W/m²·K). The process engineer’s question: does the part get below 200 °C within 60 seconds? And if not — when?

title: HW 7 · The quench
text: A 1045-steel sphere, 5.0 cm diameter, leaves a furnace at 850 °C and is quenched in a large agitated water bath at 25 °C (convection coefficient \(h = 350\) W/m²·K). The process engineer’s question: does the part get below 200 °C within 60 seconds? And if not — when?

title: HW 7 · The quench
text:
Background
If the part’s interior stays nearly uniform in temperature (a real assumption — see below), an energy balance gives the rate law
\[\rho V c\,\frac{dT}{dt} = -h A\,(T - T_\infty)\]
with \(V = \pi d^3/6\), \(A = \pi d^2\). That’s a rate law, and you own a machine for rate laws: march it (week 9). Steel properties come from your own HW 2 librarian — import it; this is why you kept the file.

title: HW 7 · The quench
text:
The assumption you must audit (S2)
“Interior stays uniform” is called the lumped capacitance assumption, and it is legitimate only when conduction inside the part is much faster than convection off its surface — quantified by the Biot number, \(Bi = h L_c / k\) with \(L_c = V/A\) (\(= d/6\) for a sphere): the standard rule of thumb is \(Bi < 0.1\). Your Step 1 spec must include computing \(Bi\) and ruling on the assumption before trusting anything downstream — and your report must say what you’d have to do differently if a plastics engineer reused your program for a polymer part (\(k \approx 0.2\) W/m·K). That question is not decoration; it is the whole difference between owning a program and owning a model.

title: HW 7 · The quench
text:
Your submission
Steps 1–4. Step 3 requires all three S-disciplines: three Euler steps by hand before trusting the loop (S1/A1); the dt-halving comparison with evidence (S3-numerical); the Biot ruling (S3-physical/S2). This problem also has an exact solution, \(T(t) = T_\infty + (T_0 - T_\infty)e^{-t/\tau}\) with \(\tau = \rho c\, d /(6h)\) — use it as your final verification, and say in one sentence why we still built the marching version (hint: next month’s rate law won’t be so polite). Step 4: the answer to the engineer’s question, the cooling curve, and the polymer-part paragraph.

title: What do engineers do with computation, and why is it awesome?
text:
Welcome. Before anything else, four things a mechanical engineer can do with a computer that you may not know are possible:
These are things working engineers actually do, and this course is about making all of them yours.

title: What do engineers do with computation, and why is it awesome?
text:
The big idea
The process of creating computational tools looks roughly like this:

  The computational pipeline
  Five boxes in a row: Idea, Specification, Production, Verification, Use, connected by arrows. A curved arrow labeled Adaptation loops from Use back to Specification.
  
    
      
    
  
  
    
    Idea
    
    Specification
    
    Production
    
    Verification
    
    Use
    
    
    
    
    
    Adaptation
  

For decades, Production — actually typing the code — was the bottleneck, so intro courses like this one spent nearly all their time on it. That bottleneck is gone: AI tools produce working code from a good description in seconds. The new bottlenecks are the two highlighted boxes:
Specification means describing the problem precisely: the inputs and outputs, what has to happen in the middle, what to do at the edges. If you cannot articulate the problem, no tool — human or AI — can solve it for you.
Verification means refusing to trust a black box: sanity-checking results against hand estimates, testing edge cases, knowing the ways a program (or a model, or an AI) goes wrong.
You will still read and run and modify plenty of code in this course — you can’t verify what you can’t read. But you will be graded on whether you can think computationally: frame a problem, direct the tools, and audit the results. That is what engineers are actually hired to do.

text:
How a week works
Before class, you read one lesson on this site (30–45 minutes) — and the lessons are runnable: most code on these pages executes right in your browser, editable, no installation, no setup. (When you want more than the browser — Colab, or Python on your own machine — the getting going page has the ladder.) No videos to watch, no Canvas quiz. Instead, every lesson ends with a Bring to class box: one question you answer on paper, committed, before you arrive.
Class opens with that question. You’ll vote on it, argue with your table, and vote again. If you didn’t do the reading, you will know it, and so will your table. That’s the whole accountability system, and it works better than a quiz because you can’t outsource an argument.
Mondays are optional and yours. All semester, one weekly optional session: Base Camp early (the beginner on-ramp, plus checkpoint dress rehearsals), Side Quests later (build a tiny language model, 3D-print a parameter sweep, and more — you vote on the menu). No grades attached, ever; just hours, help, and getting to know each other.
Four Tuesdays open with a checkpoint (weeks 4, 6, 8, 10): twenty minutes, individual, on paper, no AI — where the convergent standards get demonstrated for real, with earlier items re-offered so a rough week is always repairable. Everything about how that feeds your grade is on the grading page.
The rest of class is work at the tables. Early in the semester that’s mostly short, sharp problems with right answers. Later it shifts toward open-ended problems where every table’s AI-assisted solution comes out different — and the interesting question becomes why.


The room has islands of computers for a reason. But when it’s time to argue, it’s screens down, eyes up. You’ll hear me say it a lot.
Homework runs on a four-step submission — specify, annotate, verify, report — where the code is never what’s graded. The homework page explains the format; the problems are real mechanical engineering (a beam to lighten, a siren to clock, a wind farm to site, a quench to time).

title: What do engineers do with computation?
section: Four things you may not know are possible
text:
Four things you may not know are possible
A first-year student can be forgiven for thinking “engineering computing” means suffering through syntax errors to make a ball bounce across a screen. Here is what it actually looks like:
Predict every outcome of a process. Write a function that models something — the stress in a bracket, the temperature of a battery — then call it 100 times with 100 different inputs and write every result to a file. Runtime: about one second. You have just explored the entire design space of a product before building anything.
Handle data at engineering scale. A test rig logging 100 readings per second produces 360,000 rows an hour. Excel is not going to help you here. The tools in this course will not even slow down.
Reach out and touch the world. From a few lines of code you can pull the live position of the International Space Station, read the accelerometer inside your own phone, or send a question to an AI and use its answer inside your program.
Solve the unsolvable. Most real equations in engineering have no algebraic solution — nobody can “solve for x.” Numerically, with a computer, many of them fall in milliseconds.


“Unsolvable” deserves its scare quotes. The equations governing a pendulum swinging at large angles have no closed-form solution. Engineers have been computing pendulum swings anyway for a very long time.
This course is about making these powers yours. But there’s a catch, and the catch is the whole point.

title: What do engineers do with computation?
text:
The pipeline
Creating a computational tool looks something like this:

  The computational pipeline
  Five boxes in a row: Idea, Specification, Production, Verification, Use, connected by arrows. A curved arrow labeled Adaptation loops from Use back to Specification.
  
    
      
    
  
  
    
    Idea
    
    Specification
    
    Production
    
    Verification
    
    Use
    
    
    
    
    
    Adaptation
  

The idea is always the hard part — no news there. But for the seventy years after that, production was the bottleneck: writing correct code takes time, and intro courses like this one were traditionally spent almost entirely on it.
That era is over. AI tools now produce working code from a good description in seconds. Production has, for most everyday engineering purposes, been solved.


A historical rhyme: John Backus reportedly disliked the tedium of assembly-language programming, so in the 1950s he led the team that created FORTRAN — and a generation of programmers stopped hand-writing machine instructions. Every generation, the tedious layer gets automated and the engineer moves up one level. You’re living through the next one.
So what’s left? The two highlighted boxes — and they are harder than they look.

title: What do engineers do with computation?
section: Specification: saying what you actually mean
text:
Specification: saying what you actually mean
Specification means describing the problem completely: the inputs, the outputs, what has to happen in between, and what should happen at the edges. It sounds trivial. It is the single hardest skill in this course, and it is where real engineering projects most often fail — long before any code is involved.
Here’s the uncomfortable truth about any tool that builds from your description, whether it’s an AI, a contractor, or a teammate: every gap in your specification gets filled with an assumption, and you don’t get to choose the assumption.
Try this one. A perfectly obedient, perfectly literal robot chef awaits your command:

“Make me a peanut butter sandwich.”







NoteClick to see what the robot needs to know





How many slices of bread? Which sides get peanut butter? How much? Spread with what? Should the jar be opened first? (You didn’t say.) Crusts on or off? Cut in half — diagonally? What if there’s no peanut butter: fail loudly, substitute almond butter, or go buy some? What does “done” look like?
None of these are jokes. Each is a decision, and if you don’t make it, the robot will — its way.



Now the engineering version. Compare these two problem statements:

A. “Write a function freq_shift(t, U, x0, y0, c, f) that returns the apparent frequency of a moving siren at each time in the array t, and plots it against time.”


B. “Write a program that would allow you to determine the velocity (speed and direction) of a siren.”

Statement A is a completed specification — someone already did all the thinking, and you’re just following instructions. Statement B is a problem. To attack B, you have to decide: what are the inputs? (A recording? Frequency-vs-time data?) What physics connects frequency to velocity? What are the unknowns? What should the program output, and in what form? What if the data is noisy?
In the old version of this course, you got Statement A. In this version, you get Statement B — because Statement B is what your future boss will hand you. Nobody in industry hands you Statement A; producing Statement A from Statement B is the job.

title: What do engineers do with computation?
section: Verification: refusing to trust the black box
text:
Verification: refusing to trust the black box
Verification means confirming a program does what you intended — without taking anyone’s word for it, including the AI’s, including your own.
The core moves, which we will drill all semester:
The hand estimate: before running anything, compute a rough expected answer for one simple case. A dropped wrench falls 3 meters in — pause, you can do this — about \(t = \sqrt{2h/g} \approx \sqrt{6/9.8} \approx 0.8\) seconds. If the program says 12 seconds, the program is wrong. If it says 0.78 seconds, you’ve earned a little trust.
The edge case: what happens at zero? At a negative input? When the file is empty? A program that works on the happy path and explodes at the edges is a program that will fail in the field.
The intuition check: you have years of physical intuition — heavier things don’t fall faster, sirens sound higher approaching than receding, hot coffee cools toward room temperature and not past it. That intuition is a verification instrument. This course will sharpen it, not replace it.






Important



An AI will hand you code that runs, produces a plot, and is confidently, invisibly wrong — a sign flipped, a unit mixed, an edge case botched. It will not warn you. “It ran without errors” and “it is correct” are entirely different claims, and confusing them is how engineering disasters happen.

title: What do engineers do with computation?
text:
The map of this course
Four verbs describe what engineers do with computation, and they organize everything we’ll touch:

Fetch — get real data into (and out of) your programs: sensors, files, the internet.
Process — turn raw data into meaningful quantities: functions, sweeps, big datasets.
Simulate — build models, make predictions, ask “what if,” and know when not to believe yourself.
Analyze — communicate findings honestly: good plots, stated uncertainty, defensible conclusions.

We’ll spend the most explicit time on Process and Simulate; Fetch and Analyze are woven through everything. The standards page lists exactly what you’ll be able to do under each verb — that list is your grade, so go read it.






TipThink



The pipeline diagram above should look faintly familiar if you’ve seen an engineering design loop: define the problem, generate a solution, test it, iterate. That’s not a coincidence — specify/produce/verify/adapt is the design loop, wearing computational clothes. You are not learning “a programming class thing.” You are learning how engineers attack problems.



On paper (yes, actual paper), write a specification — 5 to 10 sentences — for this problem: a program that tells a student the fastest walking route between two buildings on campus. Your spec must state the inputs, the outputs, and at least three edge cases with what should happen in each.
Class opens with tables exchanging specs and hunting for the gaps. The table that finds the most unstated assumptions in another table’s spec wins bragging rights. Bring your sharpest pedantry.
crumbs: What do engineers do with computation?

title: First contact
text: Time to touch a computer. This lesson gets you running Python code in your browser — nothing to install, nothing to configure, nothing to break.

title: First contact
text:
Think First
Recall

From last week: what does an LLM do with the gaps in your specification?
A calculator evaluates 2 + 3 * 4 as 14, not 20. What rule is it following, and did anyone ever teach it to you as a computing rule?

Look Ahead

If AI can write code, why are we about to learn to read it line by line?
What’s the difference between a program storing a value and displaying a value?

title: First contact
section: Google Colab: a lab bench in your browser
text:
Google Colab: a lab bench in your browser
Go to colab.research.google.com and sign in with your university Google account. Click New notebook. That’s the whole setup. You now have a notebook: a document made of cells, where each cell holds a bit of Python code you can run by pressing Shift+Enter (or the ▶ button).


Python runs on Google’s computers, not yours — that’s why there’s nothing to install. Your Chromebook, gaming rig, and six-year-old laptop are all equally powerful here.
Type this into the first cell and run it — or, since this page runs Python right here in your browser, edit and run it below (the first run takes a few seconds while Python loads; after that it’s instant):






The text appears below the cell. Congratulations — you are a person who has run a program. The print(...) part is a function (a named, reusable action — much more on these in week 3) whose job is displaying things. Everything between the quotes is the text it displays.

title: First contact
text:
Variables: giving numbers names
A variable is a name attached to a value, so you can use the value by its name:
g = 9.81        # gravitational acceleration, m/s^2
h = 3.0         # drop height, m


Everything after a # is a comment — a note for humans that Python ignores. Notice the comments carry the units. In this course, a number without units is a rumor.
The = sign here does not mean “equals” in the math sense. It means “store the value on the right under the name on the left.” This distinction will matter enormously, so here’s the line that looks insane to a mathematician but is everyday code:
count = count + 1
As algebra, nonsense. As an instruction — take the value stored in count, add 1, store the result back under count — perfectly sensible. Reading = as “gets” instead of “equals” will save you real confusion.

title: First contact
section: The habit that defines this course: predict, then run
text:
The habit that defines this course: predict, then run
Here is a complete little program. Before you run it — before you even think about running it — write down what you expect it to display. On paper. Committed.






(Yes, this cell runs too — but the prediction comes first, on paper. Running before predicting is watching lights blink; you’ll get nothing from it, and the only person who’d know is the only person it matters to.)


** is Python’s “raise to a power,” so x ** 0.5 is a square root. And * must always be written explicitly: 2h is an error, 2 * h is code.
Some reading help: line 3 computes \(t = \sqrt{2h/g}\) — the fall time of a dropped object, which you met last week. So before running: \(2 \times 3 / 9.81 \approx 0.61\), and \(\sqrt{0.61} \approx 0.78\). Prediction: something near 0.78.
Now run it.






NoteClick after you’ve actually run it





You should see 0.7820... — matching the hand estimate. Feel that little click of confirmation? That’s verification (standard A1), and it’s the feeling this course is built around. You didn’t trust the program because it ran; you trusted it because you predicted its behavior and it complied.
If you got an error instead — welcome to programming; see the next section.



This predict-then-run move is the single most important habit in the course. It’s how you’ll read AI-generated code, how you’ll debug, how class voting works, and how the final exam works. Running code without a prediction teaches you nothing; you’re just watching lights blink.

title: First contact
text:
Errors are data, not disasters
Delete the h = 3.0 line and run the cell again. You’ll get an angry red block ending in something like:
NameError: name 'h' is not defined
Two things to know about errors, permanently:
They are normal. Professionals generate errors all day. The difference between a beginner and an expert isn’t fewer errors — it’s that the expert reads the message. The last line usually names the problem (NameError: you used a name nothing was stored under) and an arrow points at the guilty line.
They are the friendly failure mode. A program that crashes loudly is telling you where it hurts. The dangerous program is the one from last week’s reading — the one that runs happily and produces a wrong answer in a confident voice. You will come to prefer the crash.






Tip



Error message you can’t parse? That is a genuinely excellent use of an LLM: paste the code and the full error, and ask what’s wrong. Then — habit — verify the explanation makes sense before applying the fix. Junior collaborator, remember.

title: First contact
text:
Reading before writing
You now know enough to read simple Python, which — in a course where AI does the production — is the load-bearing skill. Predict what this displays, on paper, before the answer:












NoteClick for the answer





8 — not 2. Line 2 stored the value 8 under b; it did not create a live mathematical relationship “b is twice a.” When a changed afterward, b had no reason to care. Code executes top to bottom, once, each line acting on values as they are at that moment. If you predicted 2, you read = as algebra. Extremely common, now permanently fixed.



That misreading — treating a program like a set of simultaneous equations instead of a sequence of actions in time — is the most common beginner stumble there is, and you’ve just met and defeated it in four lines.

On paper, two things:

Your committed prediction for what this displays — with one sentence of reasoning:

x = 10
y = x + 5
x = x + 1
print(x)
print(y)

Run your own falling-wrench calculation in Colab for a height of your choosing (a building you know, a cliff you’ve seen). Write down: your height, your hand estimate, and what the program said. Tuesday opens with the prediction vote, and your table will compare wrench numbers — anyone whose estimate and output disagree gets the fun job of figuring out why, live.

title: Functions: the contract
text: Everything promised in week 1 — the parameter sweep, the design-space-in-one-second — runs on a single idea: write the calculation once, name it, and call it as many times as you want. That’s a function, and it is the fundamental unit of engineering computation.

title: Functions: the contract
text:
Think First
Recall

Week 1: what are the parts of a complete specification?
Week 2: the pool script computed one pool. What would you do if your boss asked about 50 different pool designs?

Look Ahead

What should happen when a function is defined but never called?
If a variable is created inside a function, should the rest of the program be able to see it?

title: Functions: the contract
text:
Anatomy of a function






This cell is live — edit it, break it, add a Mars gravity call (\(g = 3.71\)). A function you’ve poked at is a function you understand.
Reading it: def starts a definition; fall_time is the name; (h, g=9.81) are the parameters — the inputs, with g given a default so callers can omit it; the indented body is what happens; return hands the result back to whoever called. The triple-quoted line is a docstring: the function’s specification, living inside the function.


Defining a function runs nothing. It’s writing a recipe, not cooking. Nothing happens until someone calls it: fall_time(3.0).
Calling it:
t1 = fall_time(3.0)          # our wrench: h = 3 m, Earth gravity
t2 = fall_time(3.0, 1.62)    # same drop on the Moon
Predict both values before reading on. (Roughly 0.78 s and — Moon gravity is about a sixth — roughly \(0.78\sqrt{6} \approx 1.9\) s. If your instinct said “longer on the Moon,” your instinct is a verification instrument. Told you.)

title: Functions: the contract
text:
The signature is a specification
Look at fall_time(h, g=9.81) and its docstring, and notice you know almost everything: what goes in, with what units, what comes out, what’s assumed (from rest). That’s not a coincidence — a function is a specification made executable. This is why the week-1 skill and this week’s skill are the same skill: a good spec practically writes the signature, and a prompt shaped like a spec gets you back code shaped like a contract.

Write a Python function pressure_drop(L, D, Q) returning the pressure drop in Pa for laminar water flow through a smooth pipe of length L (m), diameter D (m), at flow rate Q (m³/s). Assume 20 °C water. Include a docstring stating the formula and its valid range.

Compare that to “write me a pipe pressure program” and predict which one comes back needing fewer repairs.

title: Functions: the contract
section: Check it in isolation — the P1 discipline
text:
Check it in isolation — the P1 discipline
Before a function enters any larger program: call it once with a case you can check by hand.
print(fall_time(3.0))   # hand estimate said ~0.78 — confirm before proceeding
This is non-negotiable, and here’s the engineering argument: next week you’ll call functions inside loops, 100 times. A sweep doesn’t just use a bug — it amplifies it 100×, and buries it in a CSV where it looks like data. One isolated hand-check beforehand is the cheapest insurance in this course.

title: Functions: the contract
section: Local names: the function’s private scratchpad
text:
Local names: the function’s private scratchpad
Predict, on paper, before the answer:












NoteClick for the answer





5. The result inside double is local — it exists only while the function runs, in the function’s private workspace, and it is a different variable from the outer result despite the shared name. This is a feature, not a hazard: it means you can use a function without knowing or caring what names it uses internally. The contract is inputs → output; the interior is private. (It’s also why you can safely use AI-written functions whose internals use ugly names.)

title: Functions: the contract
text:
Bring functions and AI together
The workflow that carries the rest of the semester: spec the function → prompt for it → annotate the body → hand-check it in isolation → only then, use it. Notice production is one step out of five, and it’s the one you delegated.






TipThink



The docstring says what the function promises. The annotation says what the body actually does. Verification is checking that those two are the same document.



Pick one from the menu — (a) pressure drop in a pipe, (b) deflection of a cantilevered beam under a tip load, (c) a °F/°C/K temperature converter — and on paper write: the full signature with units, a two-sentence docstring including assumptions, and one hand-checkable test case with its expected output (show the arithmetic). Thursday you’ll direct the AI to build it and your committed test case becomes the acceptance test. If the AI’s function fails your test, one of you is wrong — and finding out which is the whole game.

title: Loops, arrays & parameter sweeps
text: This is the payoff week. Week 1 promised you could predict all the outcomes of a process in one second. Today you collect.

title: Loops, arrays & parameter sweeps
text:
Think First
Recall

Week 3: why did we insist a function be hand-checked in isolation before use? (This week you’ll see the stakes.)
Week 4: what makes a while loop stop?

Look Ahead

A loop runs a calculation 100 times. Where do 100 results go?
If one run takes 0.01 seconds, what’s stopping you from trying a million designs?

title: Loops, arrays & parameter sweeps
section: The for loop: repetition over a collection
text:
The for loop: repetition over a collection






Read: “for each value in heights, calling it h, run the indented block.” Four values, four passes, four printed lines. The loop variable h takes each value in turn.
The accumulator pattern — building something up across passes — is the one to drill:






Trace it on paper: total goes 0 → 1 → 4 → 14 → 44. There’s your count = count + 1 from week 2, finally earning its keep. And range(5) manufactures the sequence 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 when you just need “do this five times.”

title: Loops, arrays & parameter sweeps
section: Arrays: a thousand values in one variable
text:
Arrays: a thousand values in one variable
NumPy arrays hold many numbers under one name — and arithmetic applies to all of them at once:








import numpy as np fetches a library — code written by others, which is most of engineering computing. The department’s learning objectives literally list “use third-party code.” You now do.
That one line replaces the whole first loop. When to use which? Arrays when the same arithmetic hits every value; loops when each pass involves decisions, accumulation, or steps that depend on the previous pass (foreshadowing week 9’s simulations, which must loop — the future depends on the present).

title: Loops, arrays & parameter sweeps
section: The parameter sweep: the marquee pattern
text:
The parameter sweep: the marquee pattern
Here is the pattern this course is named after. One verified function + one loop + one output file:
import csv
from my_functions import fall_time      # the function you hand-checked in week 3

heights = np.linspace(0.5, 50, 100)     # 100 heights from 0.5 to 50 m

with open("sweep_results.csv", "w", newline="") as f:
    writer = csv.writer(f)
    writer.writerow(["height_m", "fall_time_s"])     # header row
    for h in heights:
        writer.writerow([h, fall_time(h)])
Run time: well under a second. Product: a 100-row CSV mapping the entire design space of this (small) problem — which next week you’ll plot, and in week 7 you’ll learn to interrogate at 60,000-row scale. Every serious “which design is best?” question in industry has this pattern somewhere inside it.






Tip



Don’t memorize the file-writing boilerplate — that’s exactly the kind of production you delegate to the AI (“…and write the results to a CSV with a header row”). Do understand the shape: open a file, write a header, write one row per pass. You need to recognize it to verify it.

title: Loops, arrays & parameter sweeps
text:
Nested loops: sweeping two knobs
for D in diameters:          # outer loop
    for L in lengths:        # inner: runs completely, for EACH diameter
        writer.writerow([D, L, pressure_drop(L, D, Q)])
Ten diameters × ten lengths = 100 rows, every combination. Reading rule for the doubly-indented shape: the inner loop is the fast one — it finishes a full lap for every single step of the outer.

title: Loops, arrays & parameter sweeps
text:
Sweep hygiene: the P1 payoff
Now the week-3 discipline shows its teeth. A sweep is an amplifier: it takes whatever your function does and does it 100 times. Feed it a verified function, get 100 trustworthy rows. Feed it the silent pool bug from week 2 — the ×100-instead-of-×1000 — and get 100 plausible, consistent, wrong rows, formatted as data, wearing a header. Nothing about the sweep’s output reveals the problem, because the error is systematic: every row is wrong the same way. Hence the iron rule: verify once, in isolation, then sweep. Never the other order.

Two commitments on paper. (1) Trace this and commit to the printed value:
total = 0
for k in [2, 4, 6]:
    total = total + k * k
print(total)
(2) Write the spec for a sweep over your week-3 function: which parameter varies, over what range and why (physical reasoning, not vibes), how many points, and the exact header row of the output CSV. Thursday: the vote on (1), then you run (2) and plot it — the first design-space picture of your career.

title: Pandas: 60,000 rows without fear
text: Week 1 promised that engineering datasets have 60,000 rows and that Excel is not going to help you. Today: the tool that will.

title: Pandas: 60,000 rows without fear
text:
Think First
Recall

Week 6: what are the F2 questions you ask of any data file before computing?
What’s the largest spreadsheet you’ve personally scrolled through? How did that go?

Look Ahead

“Find every row where temperature exceeded 80 °C” — how would you even start in Excel with 60,000 rows?
If a program reduces 60,000 numbers to 5, how do you verify the 5?

title: Pandas: 60,000 rows without fear
text:
When spreadsheets break
Excel is genuinely good at what it’s for: small tables, quick looks, hand-entered data, one-off arithmetic. But a test rig logging 10 sensors at 100 Hz produces 60,000 rows in a minute. At that scale Excel becomes a scrolling punishment: slow, click-driven, unrepeatable — and unrepeatable is the professional disqualifier. “I clicked some filters and sorted some stuff” is not a workflow anyone can rerun, audit, or apply to next week’s file. (A3 provenance again: an analysis nobody can rerun is a rumor with formatting.)

title: Pandas: 60,000 rows without fear
text:
The DataFrame
Pandas gives you the DataFrame: a whole table living in one variable, columns addressed by name.
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("motor_test_log.csv")
df.head()          # show the first 5 rows — ALWAYS the first thing you run
head() is week 6’s “look before you compute” habit, industrialized: five rows tell you the column names, the units situation, and whether anything is obviously deranged, without printing 60,000 lines.
df["temp_C"]            # one column, by name
df["temp_C"].mean()     # one meaningful number from 60,000
df["temp_C"].max()
df.describe()           # summary statistics for every numeric column at once

title: Pandas: 60,000 rows without fear
section: Filter, summarize, reduce — the P3 verbs
text:
Filter, summarize, reduce — the P3 verbs
Filtering is week 4’s booleans, applied to an entire column at once:
hot = df[df["temp_C"] > 80]      # a new DataFrame: only the too-hot rows
len(hot)                          # how many were there?
hot["rpm"].mean()                 # what was the motor doing during them?
Read the inner part first: df["temp_C"] > 80 produces 60,000 booleans; wrapping it in df[...] keeps the rows where it’s True. Grouping answers “broken down by…” questions:
df.groupby("test_phase")["temp_C"].mean()   # average temp in each phase of the test
That’s the whole P3 skill: an engineering question in English (“how hot did it run during startup vs. cruise?”) becomes a filter, a group, and a summary — 60,000 rows in, five meaningful numbers out, in three repeatable lines.

title: Pandas: 60,000 rows without fear
text:
Try the verbs, right here
A live pandas sandbox — a different tiny dataset (your Bring-to-class miniature stays a paper exercise, on purpose):






Edit it: filter on a different threshold, group by run (and notice why that’s useless — grouping needs repeats), add a column. Two minutes of poking beats twenty of reading.

title: Pandas: 60,000 rows without fear
section: Tool choice is an engineering decision
text:
Tool choice is an engineering decision
So is Excel dead? No — and “which tool?” is itself a skill this course assesses. Quick look at a 30-row file a colleague sent? Excel, obviously; importing it into pandas would be ceremony. Repeatable analysis of instrument data? Pandas. The rule of thumb: Excel for looking, pandas for pipelines — if you’ll do it twice, or on data too big to eyeball, or anyone might ask “how did you get this?”, it’s a script.

title: Pandas: 60,000 rows without fear
text:
AI, pandas, and the spot-check
Pandas is where AI assistance genuinely shines — “group by test phase and report the mean and max temperature of each” comes back correct and idiomatic almost every time. It is also where silent wrongness thrives, because the failure modes are invisible at scale: filtering > 80 when the spec meant >= 80, grabbing temp_F when you meant temp_C, a groupby that quietly dropped rows with missing values. The verification move is the spot-check: take the AI’s five-number answer, pick one group, and verify it against a handful of rows you can inspect by eye — or better, against a miniature of the dataset where you know every answer. Which is exactly what you’re about to do.

title: Simulate I: stepping into the future
text: Week 1’s last promise: solving the “unsolvable.” Today you build a time machine out of parts you already own — and I mean that literally: this lesson contains no new Python. A function (week 3), a loop (week 5), a plot (week 6). Only the idea is new, and the idea is enormous.
crumbs: Simulate I: stepping into the future

title: Simulate I: stepping into the future
text:
Think First
Recall

Week 5: when must you use a loop instead of array arithmetic? (Hint: when each pass depends on the one before.)
Hot coffee on your desk: does it cool faster at the start or near the end? Why do you believe that?

Look Ahead

If you know a system’s rate of change right now, how far into the future dare you predict?
Two simulations of the same coffee disagree. How do you decide which — if either — to trust?
crumbs: Simulate I: stepping into the future

title: Simulate I: stepping into the future
text:
Two kinds of model
Everything so far evaluated algebraic relations: plug in \(h\), get fall time. Question in, answer out, done. But most engineering systems don’t hand you an answer formula — they hand you a rule for how things change: the coffee cools at a rate proportional to how much hotter it is than the room. Physics gives the rate; you want the future. The bridge between them is the oldest trick in computational science:

New value = old value + (rate of change) × (small time step)

That’s it. That’s the time machine. Apply the rule, step forward a little, re-evaluate the rate (it changed! the coffee is cooler now), step again. March into the future one small step at a time.


This is called Euler’s method, and it’s the ancestor of every simulation you’ve ever seen — weather forecasts, car-crash models, video-game physics. They use fancier steps; the marching idea is identical.
crumbs: Simulate I: stepping into the future

title: Simulate I: stepping into the future
section: By hand first — three steps, on paper
text:
By hand first — three steps, on paper
Coffee at \(T = 90\) °C in a \(20\) °C room, cooling law \(\text{rate} = -k(T - 20)\) with \(k = 0.05\) per minute, step size \(\Delta t = 1\) minute.
Step 1: rate \(= -0.05(90-20) = -3.5\) °C/min, so \(T \leftarrow 90 + (-3.5)(1) = 86.5\). Step 2: rate \(= -0.05(86.5-20) = -3.325\), so \(T \leftarrow 86.5 - 3.325 = 83.175\). Step 3: you. (Commit before checking: rate \(= -0.05(63.175) = -3.159\), so \(T \approx 80.02\).)
Notice what your hands just learned: the rate itself shrinks as the coffee cools — fast cooling early, slow later, exactly matching your Think First intuition. The hand-march is the hand estimate (A1) for everything that follows.
crumbs: Simulate I: stepping into the future

title: Simulate I: stepping into the future
section: The code — assembled entirely from prior weeks
text:
The code — assembled entirely from prior weeks
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def cooling_rate(T, T_room=20, k=0.05):
    """Rate of temperature change (deg C per min), Newton's law of cooling."""
    return -k * (T - T_room)

dt = 1.0                      # step size, minutes
T = 90.0                      # initial condition
temps = [T]
for step in range(120):       # march 120 minutes into the future
    T = T + cooling_rate(T) * dt      # THE line: new = old + rate * step
    temps.append(T)

plt.plot(np.arange(121) * dt, temps)
plt.xlabel("Time (min)"); plt.ylabel("Coffee temperature (°C)")
Read the loop body and recognize old friends: it’s the accumulator pattern (week 5) where the thing accumulating is the future, and T = T + ... is week 2’s “gets, not equals” carrying the entire simulation on its back. This is the convergence moment of the course: nothing here is new except the power.
crumbs: Simulate I: stepping into the future

title: Simulate I: stepping into the future
section: Step size, and the first way simulations lie
text:
Step size, and the first way simulations lie
Run it again with dt = 25 (steps of 25 minutes). The simulation still runs, still plots, still looks confident — and it is now measurably wrong: each step charges 25 minutes in a straight line at a rate that was only true at the step’s start. Whether that straight-line charge lands you above or below the true curve is exactly your Bring-to-class question, so no spoilers here — but crank dt truly huge and the “coffee” can oscillate, or plunge below room temperature: a thermodynamic impossibility, rendered in a professional-looking plot.






Important



This is S3’s first failure mode — numerical error, wrongness you injected by discretizing, with no physics mistake anywhere. The standard check costs one rerun: halve the step and compare. If the answer barely moves, the step was fine. If it shifts, keep halving until it stops. A simulation whose answer depends on dt isn’t an answer yet.
crumbs: Simulate I: stepping into the future

title: Simulate I: stepping into the future
section: Verify against a known answer — while you still can
text:
Verify against a known answer — while you still can
This particular problem is one we can also solve exactly with calculus: \(T(t) = 20 + 70e^{-0.05t}\). Plot both — with dt = 1 they’re nearly indistinguishable; the marching machine works. Now the strategic point: we verified the method on a problem with a known answer because next week’s problems won’t have one. That’s the whole professional pattern — calibrate your tools where truth is available, then carry the earned trust (and the halve-the-step habit) into the wilderness where you actually need simulation. It’s also why this week’s toy problem isn’t a toy: it’s your instrument calibration.

On paper: (1) March the coffee model three steps by hand with \(\Delta t = 2\) minutes (same \(k\), same start — show the arithmetic). (2) Commit with one sentence of reasoning: the true cooling curve is concave-up (steep early, flattening); Euler steps travel in straight lines at the starting rate of each step — so does a too-big step land above or below the true curve? Thursday: build-a-model lab, where each table gets a different system to march (draining tank, falling object with drag, charging capacitor, heating apartment) and we discover every table’s model is wrong in its own special way. That’s not a bug in the plan.
