title: Your second language
text: Surprise: you’re learning MATLAB today. Bigger surprise: it will take about forty minutes, because — and this is the actual lesson — you didn’t spend ten weeks learning Python. You spent ten weeks learning computing, in a Python accent. Time to prove it.

title: Your second language
text:
Think First
Recall

P4 asks you to predict what a short script does. Does anything in that skill actually depend on the language the script is written in?
Week 2: what does an error message owe you? (Hold onto this — MATLAB’s dialect of complaint differs, but the debt is the same.)

Look Ahead

Why would a company pay real money for MATLAB when Python is free?
If an AI translates your Python to MATLAB, what exactly is your job in that transaction?

title: Your second language
section: Why a second language at all
text:
Why a second language at all
Because mechanical engineering runs on MATLAB in ways you will personally collide with: Simulink (graphical modeling of dynamic systems — the industry standard for controls), decades of validated toolboxes, and forty years of legacy code in aerospace, automotive, and every controls lab on this campus. You will inherit MATLAB code in your career whether you choose to or not. But the deeper reason is the meta-lesson: languages are choices, not identities, and an engineer who can read a language they never studied has demonstrated that the concepts live above the syntax. That’s the department’s “understand differences between languages and choose appropriately” objective — not as a bullet point, but as a lived Tuesday.

title: Your second language
text:
The Rosetta stone
The falling wrench, twice:



# Python
def fall_time(h, g=9.81):
    t = (2 * h / g) ** 0.5
    return t

heights = [1.0, 3.0, 10.0]
for h in heights:
    print(fall_time(h))


% MATLAB
function t = fall_time(h, g)
    t = sqrt(2 * h / g);
end

heights = [1.0, 3.0, 10.0];
for h = heights
    disp(fall_time(h, 9.81))
end



Read the MATLAB cold and sort what you see into three bins. Identical: the thinking — a function with a contract, a loop over values, a call per pass. You can already trace this. Cosmetic: % for comments, disp for print, end closing blocks instead of indentation, semicolons suppressing output. Learnable in an afternoon; not worth an anxiety. Genuinely different: two items only, and here they are.

title: Your second language
text:
The two real differences
Indexing starts at 1. heights(1) is the first element in MATLAB; heights[0] is the first in Python. This is the single most productive bug-generator in bilingual engineering code, because an off-by-one doesn’t crash — it quietly hands you the wrong element, which then flows through your analysis wearing a straight face (week 2’s silent-error, reborn). Every translation gets its indices audited. Every one.
Matrices are the native object. MATLAB is MATrix LABoratory: everything is a matrix, * means true matrix multiplication (you want .* for element-by-element — NumPy’s default), and linear algebra is home turf rather than an import. This is why controls and vibrations people love it, and it’s a genuine difference of worldview, not spelling.

title: Your second language
section: AI as translator — and the A4 fine print
text:
AI as translator — and the A4 fine print
LLMs translate Python↔︎MATLAB nearly flawlessly; whole-file translation is arguably their single most reliable coding trick. So the production is, as ever, delegated — and your job in the transaction is the audit: run both versions on the same hand-checkable input (your P1 test case rides again, now bilingual) and confirm the outputs match; then specifically eyeball every index and every * that should be .*, because those are precisely the seams where translation slips silently. Same doctrine as week 1, new costume: the translation ran ≠ the translation is right.

title: Your second language
section: Choosing tools: there are right answers
text:
Choosing tools: there are right answers
The framework, in priority order — What does the team/legacy code use? What libraries does the task need? What’s the lifespan? — applied to five scenarios:
Quick look at a colleague’s 30-row CSV → Excel (week 7’s ruling stands). Simulating a suspension with a controls team that lives in Simulink → MATLAB, no contest. Fetching API data, wrangling 60k rows, feeding an ML model → Python, whose ecosystem owns that pipeline. Estimating whether a pump can fill the tank by Friday → paper, thirty seconds, no computer; over-tooling is also a tool-choice error. Inheriting 5,000 lines of working, validated MATLAB → MATLAB; rewriting working validated code for language preference is how engineers set fire to a month. Note what never appeared in the framework: “which language do I like.”

Below is a MATLAB script you have never been taught to read. On paper: (1) commit to exactly what it displays; (2) flag the one line you’re least sure about and say why. Bins and indices are your friends.
vals = [4, 10, 6];
total = 0;
for v = vals
    total = total + v^2;
end
disp(total / vals(1))
Thursday is project launch: the menu, the teams, and your project’s first specification — the beginning of the artifact you’ll defend in finals. The languages unit ends where the real work begins, which is the point: from here on, the language is just whichever tool the job wants.

title: The defense
text: The final exam is a written defense of your own project: pencil, paper, a printed map of your team’s files, and questions about what is actually going on inside them. Not a coding test. Not trivia. An examination of whether you can hold the thing you built in your head — which is standard P5, resting on everything under it.

title: The defense
text:
Why this format
Because it’s the honest version of the question every reviewer of this course asked: you used AI — but do you understand it? An engineer who “built” something they can’t explain didn’t build it; they were adjacent to it. Industry’s stated expectation is exactly this: AI-assisted production is normal, and the engineer can review, validate, and modify what was produced. The defense is where those two clauses meet. It is also, notice, un-outsourceable by construction: the AI wrote code; it cannot sit in the room and be you knowing things.
One consequence worth savoring: since every exam is about your project, every exam in the room is different. There is nothing to copy, nothing to leak, no question bank to grind. The only preparation that works is the one that was the point all along.

title: The defense
text:
What the questions look like
Five species, with live examples (yours will be about your files):
Trace — “Sensor data enters in load_data.py and a damping coefficient exits in the report. Walk the data through every file it touches; name each transformation.”
Justify — “Filtering lives in its own file. Why? What specifically gets worse if it’s merged into main.py?” (Architecture has reasons; know yours. “The AI did it that way” is an answer that scores what it deserves.)
Predict — “The input CSV arrives missing its header row. What happens, where does it fail, and what does the user see?” (Week 4’s edge-case doctrine, aimed at your own creation.)
Audit — “Here’s a plausible AI-suggested change to your processing file. Would you accept it? What breaks?” (A4, inverted: now you’re reviewing the AI’s PR against a codebase you must actually know.)
Verify — “The report claims 0.31 for the damping ratio. Convince me. What’s the hand estimate, and how far do you trust that digit?” (A1 and A3, pointed at the number with your name on it.)

title: The defense
section: How to prepare — the secret is that you already did
text:
How to prepare — the secret is that you already did
The real preparation was distributed across the whole semester, disguised as habits: the annotation discipline (week 2) means every line entered your project with a why attached — the defense is a conversation about work you already narrated; the spec history is the answer key to every Justify question; the verification evidence is the answer key to every Verify question. Students who kept the habits study for this exam by rereading their own project for an evening. Students who didn’t will discover in week 14 that you cannot annotate three weeks of a stranger’s code — even when the stranger was you, in a hurry, in November.
Concretely, this week: reread every file and check you can still say each block’s why aloud; re-run your hand checks; do one full Trace of your main data path with the file map in front of you; and ask each teammate the Justify question about their files, because their files are on your exam too.

title: The defense
text:
Mock defenses (Thursday)
Tables run the format on each other, question bank provided: ten minutes as examinee, ten as examiner, rotate. Being the examiner is the best preparation available — the moment you try to write a hard Predict question about someone’s file structure, you understand what the format is probing, and you will hear yourself asking your own project the same questions on the drive home. Which is the course working as intended.

Write the three defense questions about your own project that you would least like to be asked. Bring them Thursday for the mock defenses. Yes, this is a trick: the act of writing them is the act of discovering exactly where your understanding is thin — four days before that information becomes expensive. You’re welcome.

title: Practice Library
text:
Every problem on this page runs in your browser — no Colab, no installs, nothing to set up. Edit the code, press Run, repeat until it’s boring. This is the one place in the course where answers sit right next to problems (this is self-study, not vote-prep), so use the hints and solutions shamelessly. The page grows as the semester does; requests welcome at any Monday session.
The first Run on this page takes a few seconds while Python loads into your browser. After that, everything is instant.

title: Practice Library
text:
Warm-up: the sandbox
Nothing to solve — just a scratchpad. Type anything, run it, break it. You cannot damage anything; reload the page and it’s factory-new.

title: Practice Library
text:
Tracing (weeks 2–3)
T1. Predict all three printed values on paper, then run to check.







Line by line, keeping a two-column table of a and b. Remember: = means gets — line 3 uses the values as they are at that moment, and b never updates afterward.


10, 4, 6. After line 1: a=6. Line 2: b=4. Line 3: a = 6+4 = 10 (b stays 4 — it stored a value, not a relationship).

T2. This one prints a single value. Commit to it before running.







The same line twice is not the same result twice — the second one starts from where the first one left off.


16. First squaring: 4. Second squaring squares the new value: 16. If you said 8, you read line 3 as “times the original x.”

title: Practice Library
text:
Functions (week 3)
F1. Fill in the blank so the function matches its docstring, then verify with the test call — it should print 78.5 (approximately).







Area is π r² — and remember Python needs the power written explicitly. Two ways to write “r squared” both work.


return 3.14159 * r ** 2      # or: 3.14159 * r * r
The verification habit in miniature: 3.14 × 25 ≈ 78.5, hand-checkable before you trust it anywhere.

F2. Predict what prints — this is the local-names idea from the week 3 reading, wearing a different shirt.







The n inside the function is the function’s private n. What happens in the function stays in the function — only the return value escapes.


1 then 11. The outer n is untouched; add_ten worked on its own local copy and shipped the result out through return.

title: Practice Library
text:
Logic (week 4)
L1. Four calls, four predictions on paper, then run.







Top to bottom, first true branch wins. And check the boundaries with a jeweler’s eye: is 100 greater than 100?


highway, highway (100 is not > 100 — the boundary lesson), too fast, city (−5 falls through to else — is that what a spec would want? That question is week 4’s whole point).

title: Practice Library
text:
Loops (week 5)
X1. Fix the loop so it prints the sum of the squares of 1 through 4 (which is 30 — verify that by hand first).







Run it as-is and look at what you get (16). The loop isn’t accumulating — each pass throws away the previous total. What’s missing from the right-hand side?


total = total + k * k
The accumulator pattern: the new total is built from the old total. total = k * k just overwrites, and you end up with only the last pass (16).

X2. Assembly problem: these lines compute the average of a list, but they’re scrambled. Reorder them (cut and paste in the editor) so it runs and prints 5.0.







Three constraints: names must exist before they’re used; the indented line belongs to the for; the print needs everything finished. (Also — could you avoid hard-coding count = 3? Python’s len(values) exists. Not required, but that’s the better program.)


values = [3, 5, 7]
total = 0
count = 3
for v in values:
    total = total + v
print(total / count)
The first three lines can go in any order among themselves — data dependency, not ceremony, dictates sequence. That observation is the entire point of assembly problems.

title: Practice Library
text:
Arrays (weeks 5–6)
A1. One line replaces the whole loop: fill in the blank so t holds the fall time for every height at once, then print it.







The formula is \(t=\sqrt{2h/g}\), and NumPy’s square root is np.sqrt(...). Write the arithmetic as if h were a single number — the array handles the “for every value” part itself.


t = np.sqrt(2 * h / 9.81)
Sanity anchor: the first entry should be ≈ 0.45 s and each height is 4× the previous, so each time should be 2× the previous (√4 = 2). Check the printout against that — a free verification pattern hiding in the problem’s structure.







Note



Want more? Say so at a Monday session or in class — this library grows in whatever direction the requests point. Solutions to homework problems will never appear here, but problems shaped like homework absolutely will.

title: Side Quests
text:
Once Base Camp winds down, Mondays keep going — same hour, same room, new flavor: Side Quests, for anyone who wants to go further than the course goes. Nothing here affects your grade, nothing is secretly required, nobody takes attendance — and by this point in the semester, Mondays are just the day we hang out and build things, which is roughly what engineering departments are for.
Dress rehearsals still claim the Mondays before checkpoints 3 and 4 (weeks 8 and 10); quests fill the rest. Which quests run is up to you — signups on Canvas; a quest runs if ~10 people want it — so consider this page a menu, not a schedule. Pitch new ones anytime; the best quests come from what you ask for. Every quest that runs leaves behind a one-page recipe on this site, so the menu grows into a library.

title: Side Quests
text:
The menu
Starting from scratch. (Timed for week 11, right before project launch.) The blank-page protocol: what to actually do when there’s no template, no starter code, and no instructions — which is your project in four days, and most of your career. The protocol is teachable: restate the problem in one sentence; name inputs and outputs; find the smallest version that could possibly work; build that; grow it. We’ll start something real from nothing, live, mistakes included.
Git & version control. (Week 12 — your project just became multi-person.) How real teams avoid final_v2_ACTUAL_final.py: commits, history, branches, and undo-anything confidence. Teams that adopt it in week 12 thank themselves in week 13.
Build a tiny language model. You’ve directed LLMs all semester; now build the ancestor — a Markov text generator, ~30 lines. Feed it a book from Project Gutenberg, watch it babble plausibly, and feel the week-1B lesson click permanently: next-chunk prediction, that’s the whole trick. The single most course-resonant hour on this menu.
Parametric design → 3D print. Code that generates geometry: a bracket with parameterized dimensions, swept over a design variable — and then we print the winner on the department’s machines. It’s HW 3’s parameter sweep made physical: the design space in your hand. (Print queue permitting; small parts.)
Measure the world. The room is full of instruments. Signal off a function generator, capture it on an oscilloscope, and record the same tone with Phyphox — then reconcile the two in Python. Fetch (F1) meets real lab hardware, and a quiet preview of your instrumentation courses.
Your data, your problem. Bring any dataset you actually care about — fantasy football, workout logs, your bank’s CSV export — and we’ll wrangle it with pandas together. The fastest way to make week 7 permanent is to point it at something you love.
Debugging as detective work. A structured method for “it’s broken and I don’t know why”: isolate, hypothesize, test, repeat. The scientific method wearing a hoodie.
ML taster, on your own data. Train a walk-vs-run classifier on your week-8 accelerometer recordings — your data, your body, ~20 lines of scikit-learn. An honest trailer for where computational coursework goes next.
Run an LLM on your own machine. Local models: what a laptop can do (more than you think), what it costs (nothing), why you might want one (privacy, no subscription, tinkering). Live setup included.
The portfolio. (Late semester.) Your project report is already a Quarto page; this session makes it a public site on GitHub Pages, plus the resume bullet that honestly describes what you did (“directed and audited AI-generated analysis of…”). The session where A3-quality documentation starts paying you back.
Where this goes next. (Week 14 / on demand.) Computational Methods, machine learning, CFD, the clubs and competitions on this campus — and a pointer at Advent of Code, which starts December 1st, the week this course ends, and is the best “how do I keep going?” answer that exists.
